0.title: Song of Songs: Love Strong as Death
0.overview:
The message. The Song of Songs is God’s gift of a love song. It sings of a bride and her bridegroom: their longing, their delight, their losing and finding each other, and the joy of their marriage, and it sings frankly and without shame, because the Creator is not embarrassed by what he made. It also guards that love for its time and for one person only, for “love is strong as death” and “Many waters cannot quench love” (8:6–7). And because Scripture calls marriage a picture of Christ and his church, the Song lifts the heart to a greater love still: the Bridegroom who gave himself for his bride and will never let her go.

Background: the title and the writer. The book opens, “The Song of Songs, which is Solomon’s” (1:1). “Song of Songs” is built like “King of kings”: the song above all songs. The words “which is Solomon’s” can mean by Solomon, for him or about him. Solomon reigned from about 970 to 930 BC, and “his songs were 1,005” (1 Kings 4:32), so tradition counted this one among them. Solomon is named in the poem (3:7–11; 8:11–12), and its places run from Lebanon and Hermon in the north to Engedi by the Dead Sea, the length of Solomon’s kingdom. Tirzah is set beside Jerusalem as a byword for beauty (6:4), and Tirzah was a royal city until about 880 BC, when the northern kings left it for Samaria, which some take as a sign of an early date. Others point to words that seem borrowed from Persian or Aramaic, such as the word for “orchard” (4:13), and date it centuries later, with Solomon as its subject, not its author. Certainty is not possible, and the message does not depend on it. This commentary takes the title at its word: the Song belongs to Solomon’s court and may well be his own, perhaps from his early years. Yet it does not hold up Solomon’s life as the pattern: the king whose “wives turned away his heart” (1 Kings 11:3) is gently put in his place at the end, where the bride prizes her one vineyard above his thousand pieces of silver (8:11–12).

The kind of writing. The Song is lyric poetry, a cycle of love songs: not law, history or prophecy, and not a story told in strict order. Like the love songs of ancient Egypt, it calls the beloved “my sister” (4:9). It speaks in pictures of gardens and vineyards, spices and wine, gazelles and doves, and several poems praise the beloved part by part (4:1–7; 5:10–16; 6:4–9; 7:1–9). The pictures are meant to be felt, not decoded. The speakers are the bride, her beloved and the young women of Jerusalem; the ESV’s labels She, He and Others are the translators’ additions, worked out from the Hebrew word forms. In a world that often treated women as property, the bride speaks first, last and most. God is named, if at all, only once, in “the very flame of the LORD” (8:6). Yet the whole book stands within his gift of marriage, and it sits beside Proverbs and Ecclesiastes as wisdom: wisdom about love.

How the book makes its case. Two refrains mark the way: the charge “that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases” (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), and the cry of belonging, “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (2:16; 6:3; 7:10). The Song opens in the middle of desire: the bride, dark from labour in her brothers’ vineyards, longs for him, and each calls the other beautiful [1:1–2:7]. He comes leaping over the hills to call her into the spring; then by night she searches the city for him and finds him [2:8–3:5]. Next comes the wedding: the king’s procession, “on the day of the gladness of his heart” (3:11), and the wedding night, where she is “A garden locked” (4:12), opened gladly to him (4:16); near the middle of the book a voice blesses the feast [3:6–5:1]. Then loss: she is slow to open to him, he is gone, she searches at cost, and her portrait of him ends, “This is my beloved and this is my friend” (5:16) [5:2–6:3]. He returns without a word of reproach; she is “the only one” (6:9), and the refrain reaches its deepest form, “his desire is for me” (7:10) [6:4–8:4]. The summit follows: love is a seal on the heart, strong as death, and cannot be bought; and the Song ends not with a conclusion but a call, “Make haste, my beloved” (8:14) [8:5–14]. So love moves from longing to union, through loss to deeper belonging, and is still reaching at the end.

Love poetry or allegory? For most of history Jews and Christians read the Song as an allegory. Jewish teachers read it as the love of God and Israel (Rabbi Akiva called it the holy of holies of Scripture), and it is still read at Passover. Origen read it of Christ and the soul; Bernard of Clairvaux preached eighty-six sermons on it and reached only chapter 3; Puritans such as Richard Sibbes and James Durham found deep comfort in it as the love of Christ and his church. They had a real reason in Scripture’s own picture of God as husband. But the book never says it is an allegory, the details can be made to mean whatever a reader wishes, and allegory can hide what God plainly says here about the goodness of married love. Some read it as a drama in which Solomon tries to win her from a shepherd lover. This commentary’s view is that its first meaning is the plain one, the love of husband and wife, physical delight included; that king and shepherd are two pictures of the same beloved; and that the Song is heard with the echo of Christ and his church that all marriage carries.

Where it leads: to Christ. The New Testament never quotes the Song, and it is not a prophecy, so Christ must not be forced into its details. It leads to him by pattern. God made marriage from the beginning to be a picture of his love for his people: “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). Jesus called himself the bridegroom (Mark 2:19), and Paul says of marriage, “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). It leads to him, too, by the need it exposes. The Song bears the name of a king whose love failed; in Jesus “something greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42), a Son of David who loved one bride and “gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). His love truly is strong as death: he went into death to win her, and he will present her “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27), until he can say, “there is no flaw in you” (4:7). The Bible ends at a wedding, for “the marriage of the Lamb has come” (Revelation 19:7), and the bride’s last cry, “Make haste, my beloved”, becomes the church’s, “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

For us. The Song tells husbands and wives that their love, bodily delight included, is God’s good gift, worth tending through every flood. It tells the young to guard the gift and not awaken love before its time; where it has not been kept, the Bridegroom’s love still forgives and makes clean. The single who long to marry, the widowed, and those wounded by abuse or betrayal may find it painful. No one is less a Christian for lacking what it describes, abuse is never part of the love it praises, and anyone in danger should seek safety at once. For every believer, married or not, belongs to the Bridegroom whose love the Song echoes, and may say to him what the bride says: “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me” (7:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Song of Songs and the First Longing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Song begins with desire, and with a woman’s voice. After the title, which calls this the finest of songs and links it to Solomon (v. 1), the bride longs for her beloved’s kisses, praising a love sweeter than wine and a name that draws others to him like perfume (vv. 2–3). She asks him to draw her after him; he brings her into his chambers, and friends rejoice with them (v. 4). From its first lines the Song treats married love as a good gift: eagerly desired, spoken without shame, and celebrated by the whole community.
verseByVerse.theology: The Bible's great love song opens with desire that is honest, joyful and directed to one beloved.

verseByVerse.quote: The Song of Songs, which is Solomon's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the song above all songs, a love song celebrating the love of husband and wife. The title is built like “King of kings”. Solomon’s songs were 1,005 (1 Kings 4:32), and this one is given the title. It has no law, history or prophecy, and God is named, if at all, only once, in “the very flame of the LORD” (8:6).

How should a Christian read it? First, as what it plainly is: a celebration of love between husband and wife. God made man and woman for each other, to become one flesh, naked and unashamed (Genesis 2:24–25), and this book sings of that gift. “Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). A church embarrassed by this book is more prudish than God.

Christ and the church. Second, because Scripture calls marriage a picture of something greater, the Song lifts our eyes: “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). It is not a code in which every detail stands for a doctrine, but a love song that, read with the whole Bible, makes the heart long for the love every marriage pictures (see the introduction).

Uncertain wording. In “which is Solomon’s” the Hebrew can mean by, for or about Solomon. This commentary takes the Song to belong to his court and perhaps to be his own (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: The speaker labels (She, He, Others) are added by translators, who work them out from the Hebrew word forms (ESV note at 1:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine; your anointing oils are fragrant; your name is oil poured out; therefore virgins love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Song opens with a woman longing for her beloved, whose love delights her more than wine.

Let him kiss me. It is the woman who speaks first. In a world that often treated women as property, the Bible’s love song opens with a woman’s longing, spoken without shame. She begins speaking about him and ends speaking to him, the way love does when the beloved comes near. His love is sweeter, more gladdening, than the best the table can offer.

Your name is oil poured out. In Scripture a name stands for character and reputation. His is like perfumed oil poured out: it spreads, and others are drawn to him too. He is worthy of love, and she knows it.

The royal bridegroom. Many have thought here of the royal bridegroom of Psalm 45, a psalm the New Testament applies to Christ (Hebrews 1:8–9): “You are the most handsome of the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips” (Psalm 45:2). Christians have often borrowed her words to say that the love of Christ is better than wine, and that we are drawn to him because his love came first: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Draw me after you; let us run. The king has brought me into his chambers. We will exult and rejoice in you; we will extol your love more than wine; rightly do they love you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She longs for him to lead her, he brings her into his own rooms, and their friends rejoice with them. Love is not reluctant. To the woman who loves him, her husband is a king.

We will exult. The others’ joy shows that married love is private, and also something the community celebrates, as every wedding feast says.

A prayer to Christ. Christians have long made “Draw me after you; let us run” their own prayer. We do not come to Christ on our own: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). But when he draws, we run. When did you last run to him, rather than drag your feet?

King or shepherd? He is called both (vv. 4, 7). Some see two men, Solomon as the rival of a shepherd lover; others take the bridegroom to be Solomon himself. Most likely “king” and “shepherd” are two pictures of one beloved: royal in honour, close as a shepherd (see the introduction).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love does not wait for its beloved to feel lovely. The bride turns to the young women of Jerusalem, conscious of skin darkened by work in the vineyards her angry brothers forced on her, yet she insists that she is lovely (vv. 5–6). Then she asks her beloved, pictured as a shepherd, where he rests his flock at noon, for she will not go looking among other men’s flocks like a woman of doubtful character (v. 7). The answer comes back gently, perhaps teasingly: follow the tracks of the flock, “O most beautiful among women” (v. 8). The woman who asked not to be stared at is called the most beautiful of all.
verseByVerse.theology: Love sees and delights in the one who feels unseen and unlovely.

verseByVerse.quote: I am very dark, but lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the curtains of Solomon. Do not gaze at me because I am dark, because the sun has looked upon me. My mother's sons were angry with me; they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!
verseByVerse.commentary:
She feels unlovely, darkened by work in the sun, yet dares to call herself lovely, because she is loved. Her words carry both embarrassment and confidence.

Dark, but lovely. The tents of Kedar were the black goat-hair tents of desert nomads; the curtains of Solomon were rich royal hangings. She is dark like the one, and lovely like the other.

Do not gaze at me. Her angry brothers sent her to labour in the vineyards, and in a court where beauty probably meant pale, pampered skin, she looks like a field worker. Busy with theirs, she has had no time for “my own vineyard”, herself. Many know that feeling: the mother who feels she has let herself go, the person shamed by family who carries it into every room.

But lovely. Love does not wait for us to become beautiful before it delights in us. Christ did not love a church that was already spotless; he loved her “so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). His love makes lovely.

Is this about race? She gives the reason herself: “the sun has looked upon me” (v. 6). Her unease is at being looked down on as a country labourer. Scripture never treats skin colour as a measure of worth: God “made from one man every nation of mankind” (Acts 17:26).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew joining word can mean “but” or “and”: she may be saying “dark and lovely”. “My own vineyard” most likely means herself (compare 8:12).
verseByVerse.note: Kedar was a nomadic tribe of the Arabian desert, known for black goat-hair tents.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you make it lie down at noon; for why should I be like one who veils herself beside the flocks of your companions? If you do not know, O most beautiful among women, follow in the tracks of the flock, and pasture your young goats beside the shepherds' tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She wants her beloved and no one else, and asks where to find him.

You whom my soul loves. The phrase will return again and again (3:1–4). She pictures him as a shepherd and wants to find him at the midday rest. She will not wander among other shepherds’ flocks like a veiled woman looking for company, who might be taken for a woman of doubtful reputation (as Tamar was, Genesis 38:14–15).

Follow in the tracks of the flock. The answer comes lightly, perhaps teasingly, and calls her “most beautiful among women”: the woman who had just asked not to be gazed at.

The shepherd who makes his flock lie down. The picture is familiar from the Psalms: “He makes me lie down in green pastures” (Psalm 23:2). And Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14). Many Christians have heard a further word here: the soul that loves Christ wants to know where he is, and he is found among his flock, his people.

Uncertain wording. “Veils herself” means to wrap or cover oneself, and why a veil matters is not certain: a woman of doubtful character, a mourner, or simply one who must go about hidden. Some ancient translations, reading the letters slightly differently, have “one who wanders”. Either way she will not go searching among other men.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–17 — Beautiful in Each Other's Eyes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love answers love with praise. He speaks first, comparing her to a splendid mare among Pharaoh’s chariots and promising her ornaments of gold and silver (vv. 9–11). She answers with fragrance: he is nard filling the room, myrrh kept close to her heart, henna blossom in the oasis of Engedi (vv. 12–14). Then the two voices meet. He says, “Behold, you are beautiful, my love” (v. 15); she says the same back to him, and their meeting place beneath cedar and pine becomes a home (vv. 16–17). Love here is mutual, spoken aloud and glad.
verseByVerse.theology: Married love is a delight each gives the other in words as well as in presence.

verseByVerse.quote: I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots. Your cheeks are lovely with ornaments, your neck with strings of jewels. We will make for you ornaments of gold, studded with silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answers with praise: she stands out like a royal mare, and he will adorn her like a queen.

A mare among Pharaoh’s chariots. Pharaoh’s chariot horses were prized and richly adorned, and she stands out like that. Chariot teams were usually stallions, so some think of a mare that throws a whole troop into confusion. She said, “Do not gaze at me”; he cannot help it.

Ornaments of gold. The promised ornaments show that love pays attention to details, and the gift is for her (in Hebrew the “you” of v. 11 is one woman, ESV note). She came feeling like a field hand; she is treated like a queen.

What husbands can learn. The bridegroom speaks his admiration aloud, specifically, and he gives. Many wives have not heard such words in years. Christ speaks delight over a church that did not deserve it, and a husband cherished like that has the best reason and help to do the same.

verseByVerse.quote: While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance. My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh that lies between my breasts. My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of Engedi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She answers with delight: he is as precious and close to her as perfume kept by her heart. Her love fills the room where the king reclines.

A sachet of myrrh. Worn at the breast, it keeps its scent close day and night; so is he to her, close to her heart and never out of her thoughts. Like henna blossoms in the oasis of Engedi, he is refreshment in a dry land.

My beloved is to me. She says it twice: not what he is to others, but to her. That is how love speaks. And it is how faith speaks of Christ: not only that he is lovely, but that he is lovely to me, “the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).
verseByVerse.note: Nard was an expensive perfume from India. En-gedi is an oasis by the Dead Sea.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves. Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, truly delightful. Our couch is green; the beams of our house are cedar; our rafters are pine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each tells the other, “you are beautiful”, and wherever they are together becomes home. He says it twice, to the woman who did not want to be looked at. Love repeats itself, because the loved heart needs to hear it more than once. Her eyes are doves: soft, gentle and bright.

And she says it back. Their meeting place seems to be outdoors: the couch is green grass, the beams are cedar and the rafters pine. The whole world has become their house.

Marriage as God meant it. Here are two people who say “you are beautiful” and mean it, and find that wherever they are together is home. Such love must be tended, as the Song will show, but it begins in delight given and returned. Beneath it lies a greater delight: the LORD “will rejoice over you with gladness” (Zephaniah 3:17).

1.title: The Song of Songs: Let Him Kiss Me
1.overview:
Where we are. The Song opens with nothing but its title: no story of how the lovers met, only a bride already longing for her beloved. This chapter begins the first poem of the book (1:1–2:7), and it sets the tone for all that follows: desire spoken without shame, and love that answers it.

The message. The love of a man and his wife is God’s good gift, to be desired, spoken and enjoyed. And true love does not wait for the beloved to become beautiful before it delights in her: it sees the woman who feels dark and unlovely and calls her “most beautiful among women”, until she can say back to him, “you are beautiful”.

Why it was said. Israel lived among nations whose religions twisted sex into worship, and in a world where a woman was often treated as her family’s property (see the introduction). Here God gives his people a song in which married love is clean, mutual and glad, and in which a woman speaks first.

How the chapter makes its case. After the title (v. 1), she longs for his kisses and his name, and asks him to draw her after him, while others rejoice with them (vv. 2–4). Then she turns, self-conscious, to the women of Jerusalem: she is dark from labouring in her brothers’ vineyards, yet lovely (vv. 5–6). She asks where her shepherd rests at noon, and is gently told (vv. 7–8). He answers with praise: she is a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots, to be adorned with gold (vv. 9–11). She replies that he is fragrance kept close to her heart (vv. 12–14), and the chapter ends with each calling the other beautiful, at home together beneath cedar and pine (vv. 15–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, as the introduction explains. God made marriage to picture his love for his people, and Paul says its mystery “refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32). Christ loved a bride who was not yet lovely, and his love makes her so: he gave himself up for her “so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). And the bride’s “Draw me after you; let us run” (v. 4) has become the prayer of everyone who has found that “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

For us. Husbands and wives may delight in each other without embarrassment, and should say so aloud, specifically and often. Anyone who feels, like the bride, dark, worn or unlovely may hear the voice of a greater Bridegroom, who has set his love on his people and does not take it back.
1.theology:
God created marriage and the delight of husband and wife, and the Song celebrates that gift without shame (Gen 2:24-25; Heb 13:4). Desire within marriage is good, mutual and to be spoken (vv. 2, 15-16).

Marriage is a picture of Christ and the church (Eph 5:31-32). Read in that light, the Song shows love that comes first and draws the beloved (v. 4; 1 John 4:19), and love that delights in one who feels unlovely and makes her lovely (vv. 5-6, 15; Eph 5:27).
1.examples:
Then: in a world where women were often treated as property, Israel's love song gave the first word to a woman, and let a field-worker who felt unlovely hear herself called the most beautiful among women.

Now: many wives have not heard a specific word of admiration in years, and many people, like the bride, feel they have let themselves go. The Song shows a love that notices, says so aloud, and keeps saying it.

keyVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves.
keyVerse.note: These words answer the bride’s fear in verse 6. She asked not to be stared at; he looks at her and calls her beautiful, twice, and by verse 16 she can say the same to him. The chapter’s story is here in one sentence: love that delights in the beloved before she feels lovely, the pattern of Christ’s love for his church.

1.reflection:
The Song opens with a woman’s honest desire for her beloved, spoken without shame (vv. 2–4). Why do you think God put a book like this in the Bible? How might it correct both the world’s view of sex and an embarrassed silence about it in the church?

The bride feels stared at and unlovely (vv. 5–6), and is answered with praise (vv. 8–10, 15). Where do you feel as she does? How does Christ’s love for a church not yet spotless (Ephesians 5:25–27) speak to that?

“Draw me after you; let us run” (v. 4). What does it look like to run after Christ rather than drag your feet, and what most often slows you down?

The lovers praise each other aloud and in detail (vv. 9–17). If you are married, what would it look like to do that this week? If you are not, how could you encourage the marriages around you?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — His Banner over Me Was Love
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love delights, rests secure, and waits for its time. She calls herself a common wildflower, and he answers that she is a lily among brambles (vv. 1–2). She replies that among the young men he is an apple tree, giving shade and sweet fruit (v. 3). He brings her to the banqueting house, and the banner raised over her is love (v. 4). Faint with love, she rests in his embrace (vv. 5–6), and then, in the first of three charges, puts the young women of Jerusalem under oath not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 7). The passage that celebrates love most warmly also guards it.
verseByVerse.theology: Love protects and displays the beloved, and it must be kept for its proper time.

verseByVerse.quote: I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys. As a lily among brambles, so is my love among the young women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She thinks herself an ordinary wildflower; to him she is the one flower among thorns.

I am a rose of Sharon. Hymns have often sung these words of Christ, but here the bride says them of herself, and she is not boasting. She means a common wildflower of the coastal plain in spring: one flower among thousands.

A lily among brambles. He turns her modest words around: a lily among brambles. To him every other woman is a thorn bush. She says she is ordinary; he says she is the only one.

What love does. Love does not argue someone into self-esteem; it sees her differently and says so. That is how Christ sees his people: not as one more face in the crowd, but as his own, for “he calls his own sheep by name” (John 10:3).
verseByVerse.note: The “rose of Sharon” was probably a bulb such as a crocus or narcissus (ESV note). Sharon is the coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the young men. With great delight I sat in his shadow, and his fruit was sweet to my taste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among the young men he stands out like a fruit tree in a forest, giving her both shelter and delight. Forest trees give shade but no food; he is shade and fruit together. She rests in his protection and enjoys what he gives. A good husband is both: a shelter his wife can rest under, and a source of delight.

Refuge and sweetness. Many believers have found the same double gift in the Lord: “Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!” (Psalm 34:8).

verseByVerse.quote: He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love. Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am sick with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brings her openly to the feast, and his love for her is plain for everyone to see.

His banner over me was love. A banner was the flag that showed which company soldiers belonged to, and the banner he raises over her, telling everyone whose she is, is love. He is not ashamed of her.

Christ’s banner. Christians have long sung this line of Christ, who brings his people to his table: the banner over us is not our record but his love: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Sick with love. She is faint, and asks for raisin cakes and apples to revive her. Anyone deeply in love knows the lightheadedness, and the Song does not call it silly.

Uncertain wording. The word for “banner” is used of the standards of Israel’s tribes in the wilderness (Numbers 2), but here some render it “intention” or “look”. On any reading, his love marks her out.
verseByVerse.note: “Banqueting house” is literally “house of wine” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love’s embrace is good, and because it is so powerful it must not be awakened before its time.

His left hand is under my head. Lovers lie together, his left arm cradling her head, his right arm around her. The Song does not blush: this is the embrace of marriage, and God calls it good.

Until it pleases. At once comes a charge, repeated twice more (3:5; 8:4): the bride puts the unmarried young women under oath not to awaken this before its time.

Like a fire. Sexual love is like a fire. In the hearth of marriage it warms a home; set loose too early, it burns the house down. Do not stir it up by what you watch, read or touch, or by where you let your imagination go, before the time God has made for it. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality; that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor” (1 Thessalonians 4:3–4). It is also a word for the married person tempted to awaken desire for someone else. And God does not leave it to our willpower: his Spirit bears the fruit of self-control in his people (Galatians 5:22–23).

Washed and sanctified. And for those who did not wait, or whose purity was taken from them? Those who have sinned can be washed: “And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified” (1 Corinthians 6:11). None of us has kept desire perfectly pure, but Christ did, and his purity is counted to those who trust him. Those who were abused carry no guilt for what was done to them; the shame belongs to the abuser, and Christ receives the wounded with tenderness. Anyone still in danger should seek safety at once and tell someone they trust.

Why swear by the gazelles? They are creatures of grace and beauty: a poetic oath, not an appeal to other gods. In Hebrew the words echo the sound of “LORD of hosts” and “God Almighty”, so the bride may be swearing by God in the language of love without naming him.
verseByVerse.note: “I adjure you” means “I put you under oath” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Arise, My Love, and Come Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love comes and calls. She hears his voice before she sees him: he comes bounding over the hills like a gazelle and looks in through the lattice (vv. 8–9). He calls her to arise and come away, because winter is past and the land is in flower (vv. 10–13). He coaxes his shy dove from the cleft of the rock, longing to see her face and hear her voice (v. 14), and asks that the little foxes that spoil the blossoming vineyards be caught (v. 15). She answers with the line that sums up the Song, “My beloved is mine, and I am his”, and asks him to come to her until the day breaks (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: The beloved comes and calls; love answers, guards what is precious, and rests in mutual belonging.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of my beloved! Behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag. Behold, there he stands behind our wall, gazing through the windows, looking through the lattice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He comes eagerly, over every obstacle, and stands outside looking for her; he will not force his way in.

The voice of my beloved! A new scene. She hears him before she sees him. Mountains are nothing to him; swift as a young stag, he arrives and looks in through the lattice. He wants to see her, but he will not force the door; he calls.

Christ at the door. Many Christians have seen here a picture of how Christ comes to his people. He does not break down doors: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20).

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved speaks and says to me: "Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away, for behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth, the time of singing has come, and the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land. The fig tree ripens its figs, and the vines are in blossom; they give forth fragrance. Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He calls her to come away with him, because winter is over and the world is coming alive.

Arise, my love, my beautiful one. Come out of the house, come with me, he says, and the reason is spring. In Israel winter is the season of cold rains; now it is over, and everything is coming to life: flowers, birdsong, figs, vine blossom. The world is new, and he wants to enjoy it with her, ending as he began: “come away”.

Winters in marriage. Marriages go through winters: seasons of grief, illness, distance, dullness. This is a call to notice when spring comes, and to go out into it together. When did you last say to your husband or wife, come away with me?

A greater spring. For the believer a greater spring is coming. The winter of this fallen world will end, and the one who loves his church will call her to come away with him into a world made new: “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

Uncertain wording. The word translated “singing” (v. 12) may instead mean “pruning”, the season when vines are cut back for growth (ESV note). Either way, the season has turned.

verseByVerse.quote: O my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the crannies of the cliff, let me see your face, let me hear your voice, for your voice is sweet, and your face is lovely.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He longs to see the face and hear the voice of his shy beloved, and coaxes her out gently.

O my dove, in the clefts of the rock. She is a shy dove hiding in a crevice of the rock. He does not drag her out; he tells her what he wants, to see her face and hear her voice, and why: her voice is sweet and her face lovely.

Let me hear your voice. Some people hide from those who love them, afraid to be seen or heard, and love coaxes them out gently. So does the Lord with timid hearts. He wants to hear your voice in prayer, not because he needs information, but because he delights in you.

verseByVerse.quote: Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards, for our vineyards are in blossom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love must be protected from the small things that quietly destroy it.

The little foxes that spoil the vineyards. Small animals got into the vineyards in spring and destroyed the blossoms before the grapes could form. The couple’s love is a vineyard in blossom.

Little foxes in marriage. It is seldom the great disasters that destroy a marriage. It is the little foxes: the unkind word left unapologised for, the screen that takes the evening, the small resentments, the busyness, the neglect. “Catch the foxes for us”: it is a shared job. Name the little foxes in your own marriage, or friendship, or walk with God, and catch them before they spoil the fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies. Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, turn, my beloved, be like a gazelle or a young stag on cleft mountains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the heart of the Song: she and her beloved belong to each other. She longs for him to be near until the night is over.

My beloved is mine, and I am his. This is mutual belonging: not ownership as control, but the belonging promised in marriage, where each gives himself to the other. “He grazes” may be rendered “he pastures his flock” (ESV note): he is still the shepherd, among the lilies.

The refrain returns. The line will return, reversed, “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine” (6:3), and again, “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me” (7:10). First she speaks of possessing him, then of belonging to him, and finally of resting in his desire for her. Love matures from “he is mine” to “I am his”.

The movement of faith. That is the movement of faith too. The believer begins by rejoicing that Christ is his, and grows into the deeper joy of belonging to Christ, who says of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

Until the day breathes and the shadows flee. Until the morning breeze comes and the night shadows go, she asks him to come to her, swift as a gazelle.

Uncertain wording. “Turn” may mean “turn to me” or “turn away”, inviting him to stay or sending him off until morning; the invitation is likelier. “Cleft mountains” may be a place name, “mountains of Bether” (ESV note); some take them as a picture of the bride herself (compare 4:6; 8:14).

2.title: My Beloved Is Mine, and I Am His
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 completes the Song’s first poem (1:1–2:7), which ends with the first charge not to awaken love before its time, and opens the second (2:8–3:5), in which the beloved comes to call his bride out into the spring.

The message. Love is a delight to be enjoyed and a fire to be guarded. The bride rests secure under her beloved’s love, and in the same breath warns that love must wait for its time. Then he comes for her and calls her out of hiding into a new season, and the chapter ends with the line that holds the whole Song: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.”

Why it was said. Young Israelites felt the pull of desire long before marriage, and lived among peoples who gave it free rein (see the introduction). The Song neither shames that desire nor lets it run wild: it praises love fully and guards it carefully.

How the chapter makes its case. She calls herself an ordinary wildflower; he calls her a lily among brambles, and she calls him an apple tree among the trees of the forest (vv. 1–3). He brings her to the banqueting house under the banner of his love, and faint with love, held in his embrace, she charges the young women not to awaken love until it pleases (vv. 4–7). Then he comes bounding over the hills and calls through the lattice, “Arise, my love”, for winter is past (vv. 8–13). He coaxes his shy dove to show her face, and asks that the little foxes be caught before they spoil the vineyards (vv. 14–15). She answers with the refrain of belonging, and asks him to come to her until the day breaks (vv. 16–17).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern. The beloved who brings his bride to his table with love as a banner over her, who comes over the mountains and calls her out of winter, is a picture of the Bridegroom who came to his people and calls them to himself: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock” (Revelation 3:20). The belonging of verse 16 finds its fullest form in him: “I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14). And beyond this world’s winter he will call his bride to come away with him into a world made new.

For us. Husbands and wives should rest in each other’s love, guard it from the little foxes, and go out together when spring comes. The unmarried are told to let love wait for its time, and those who did not wait are told that Christ washes. Every believer may say of Christ, with even greater certainty, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.”
2.theology:
Married love is a protecting, public and delighting love (vv. 3-4), and its physical expression is good (v. 6; Heb 13:4). Desire must not be awakened before its time; sexual purity is God's will (v. 7; 1 Thess 4:3-5).

Love must be guarded against small threats (v. 15). Husband and wife belong to each other in covenant (v. 16; 1 Cor 7:4). Christ's love is a banner over his people (v. 4; Rom 5:8); he comes and calls rather than forces (vv. 8-9; Rev 3:20), and his people belong to him (John 10:14).
2.examples: She sees herself as one crocus among thousands on the plain; he sees a lily among brambles. Desire is like fire: in the hearth it warms the house, loose in the house it burns it down. And the foxes that spoil a marriage are usually small, like the screen that quietly takes every evening.

keyVerse.quote: My beloved is mine, and I am his; he grazes among the lilies.
keyVerse.note: This is the Song’s refrain of belonging, heard here for the first time and returning in 6:3 and 7:10. It says what marriage is: two people given wholly to each other. And it is what every believer may say of Christ, with even greater certainty, because he has made us his own and no one will snatch us out of his hand (John 10:28).

2.reflection:
She calls herself an ordinary wildflower; he calls her a lily among brambles (vv. 1–2). How does the way someone who loves us sees us change the way we see ourselves? How does Christ see his people?

The passage that celebrates love most warmly also says, “that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases” (v. 7). Why do the two belong together? What practical guards does that call for, in your life or in the lives of the young people you know?

What are the “little foxes” (v. 15) that threaten your marriage, your friendships or your walk with God? How could you catch them together?

“My beloved is mine, and I am his” (v. 16). What difference does it make to know not only that Christ is yours, but that you are his?

3.text: <sup>1</sup>On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not.<sup>2</sup>I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but found him not.<sup>3</sup>The watchmen found me as they went about in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?"<sup>4</sup>Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.<sup>5</sup>I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.<sup>6</sup>What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of a merchant?<sup>7</sup>Behold, it is the litter of Solomon! Around it are sixty mighty men, some of the mighty men of Israel,<sup>8</sup>all of them wearing swords and expert in war, each with his sword at his thigh, against terror by night.<sup>9</sup>King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon.<sup>10</sup>He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.<sup>11</sup>Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — I Sought Him Whom My Soul Loves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love seeks the beloved until it finds him, and then holds on. On her bed at night she seeks “him whom my soul loves” and does not find him (v. 1). She will not lie still: she rises, searches the streets and squares, and asks the watchmen (vv. 2–3). Just past them she finds him, holds him fast and brings him home to her mother’s house (v. 4). Then, as in 2:7, she charges the young women of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 5). Longing this strong is exactly why love must be kept for its time.
verseByVerse.theology: Love that has known the beloved cannot rest in his absence; it seeks until it finds and holds fast.

verseByVerse.quote: On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but found him not. I will rise now and go about the city, in the streets and in the squares; I will seek him whom my soul loves. I sought him, but found him not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parted from him by night, she aches for the one she loves, and instead of waiting she gets up to look for him.

On my bed by night. She reaches for him, and he is not there. Whether this is a dream, a memory of the days before the wedding, or simply the ache of absence, the feeling is plain: longing. “Him whom my soul loves” comes four times in verses 1 to 4; she cannot speak of him without saying what he means to her.

I will rise now and go about the city. She does not lie still and wait for the feeling to pass, but goes out into the dark city to look for him, improper as that was for a young woman at night. Love makes people bold.

Nights of the soul. Believers know nights like this, when the sense of God’s nearness is gone. Isaiah prayed, “My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you” (Isaiah 26:9). The right response is not to roll over and wait, but to rise and seek him in his word, in prayer and among his people: the means he has given for finding him.

For the widowed. For the widowed, reaching across the bed and finding no one may be all too literal. The Song does not mock that grief, and the Lord who is “near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18) does not leave the bereaved alone in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: The watchmen found me as they went about in the city. "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?" Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves. I held him, and would not let him go until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She searches until she finds him, and then she holds him and will not let him go.

The watchmen found me. She does not even explain herself. She simply asks, “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”, as if everyone must know who she means. Love assumes the whole world knows the beloved.

I held him, and would not let him go. Just past them, there he is. She brings him home to her mother’s house, the place of safety and belonging. Having found him after such a night, she will not lose him again.

Holding on. Jacob wrestled through the night and said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me” (Genesis 32:26). Mary Magdalene went looking in the dark for the body of her Lord; when he spoke her name she held on to him, and he said, “Do not cling to me”, because he had not yet ascended to the Father (John 20:15–17). The risen Christ is now found by faith, and faith holds him and will not let him go. Beneath our hold on him is a firmer hold: he holds us.

verseByVerse.quote: I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles or the does of the field, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because longing is so powerful, love must not be stirred up before its time.

Desire and its warning. The refrain of 2:7 returns word for word, straight after a scene of intense longing. No book of the Bible celebrates desire more openly than the Song, and it also warns, more than once, against awakening it too soon. Those who treasure love most will guard it most carefully.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The waiting gives way to a wedding. A column of perfumed smoke rises from the wilderness: it is Solomon’s litter, coming in splendour (vv. 6–7). Sixty of Israel’s best warriors surround it, swords ready against the terrors of the night (vv. 7–8). The king’s carriage is made of cedar from Lebanon, with posts of silver, a back of gold and a seat of purple, its inside lovingly furnished by the women of Jerusalem (vv. 9–10). Then the daughters of Zion are called out to see King Solomon in the crown his mother gave him on his wedding day, “the day of the gladness of his heart” (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: The wedding day is the king's day of gladness, and all are called out to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: What is that coming up from the wilderness like columns of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the fragrant powders of a merchant?
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wedding procession appears, rising out of the wilderness in a cloud of perfume: something glorious is coming.

What is that coming up from the wilderness? A new and grand scene. From a distance all anyone can see is smoke rising like pillars, and all anyone can smell is myrrh, frankincense and costly spices.

Like columns of smoke. To Israelite ears this might recall the pillar of cloud that led their fathers through the desert: perhaps only an echo, but it lends the moment glory.

Who is in the litter? Verse 7 calls it Solomon’s, and the bride is most likely carried in it to meet the king on his wedding day (v. 11). Either way it pictures the royal honour of the wedding, whether or not it describes Solomon’s own marriage.

Uncertain wording. The question can also be translated “Who is this…?”, as of the bride in 8:5; the Hebrew “this” is feminine, which fits either the bride or the litter.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it is the litter of Solomon! Around it are sixty mighty men, some of the mighty men of Israel, all of them wearing swords and expert in war, each with his sword at his thigh, against terror by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The procession is carried in safety, guarded by the best of Israel’s warriors.

Sixty mighty men. Sixty warriors, the best of Israel’s soldiers, surround the king’s litter, armed “against terror by night”: bandits on the road, attackers in the dark. The king protects what he loves, and a husband who loves his wife makes her safe.

Against terror by night. A psalm of God’s protection over his people uses the same picture: “You will not fear the terror of the night” (Psalm 91:5).
verseByVerse.note: A “litter” is a couch carried by servants (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon. He made its posts of silver, its back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s carriage is splendid, but its finest feature is the love worked into it.

King Solomon made himself a carriage. “Carriage” may be rendered “sedan chair” (ESV note). It was built of cedar from Lebanon, the finest timber of the ancient world and the wood of the temple itself, with silver posts, a gold back and a purple seat. And the inside was “inlaid with love” by the women of the city, perhaps with embroidery made as a wedding gift. The most beautiful thing about it was not the gold but the love.

Inlaid with love. A home can be furnished with silver and gold and still be cold. What makes the inside beautiful is love worked into it, day by day, by the people who live there.

Uncertain wording. The word for “carriage” occurs only here in the Old Testament and may be borrowed from another language. “Inlaid with love” is also hard: some suggest a word for leather or inlay work rather than “love”, but “love” is the plain reading and suits the Song.

verseByVerse.quote: Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king’s wedding day is named as the day his heart was glad, and the whole city is called to share his joy.

The day of the gladness of his heart. The king wears a wedding crown given by his mother. Of all the days of Solomon’s reign, with its wealth and wisdom and temple building, this one is named as the day his heart was glad. Psalm 45 describes a royal wedding in the same spirit, where the bride is “led to the king”, “With joy and gladness” (Psalm 45:14–15).

Another Bridegroom. Scripture points to another Bridegroom and another wedding. Jesus told of the cry at midnight, “Here is the bridegroom! Come out to meet him” (Matthew 25:6). The only crown this King was given on earth came from soldiers: “the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head” (John 19:2). Yet even that day hid a gladness: he went to the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2), the joy of a Bridegroom winning his bride. Scripture’s last pages speak of “the marriage of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:7), and on that day the gladness of his heart will be complete.

3.title: Him Whom My Soul Loves
3.overview:
Where we are. The second poem, which began with the beloved calling his bride out into the spring (2:8), closes here with a night search and the refrain of 2:7 (3:1–5). Then the third poem begins, the wedding, which runs to 5:1: the royal procession comes into view (3:6–11).

The message. Love seeks the beloved and, once it finds him, holds on; and love this strong must be guarded until its time. Then the waiting ends in a wedding, and the king’s wedding day is called “the day of the gladness of his heart”. In God’s world a wedding is one of the gladdest days there is.

Why it was said. In Israel a wedding was a public, joyful, family affair, with a procession, a crown and a feast (see the introduction). By setting the lovers’ union inside a royal wedding, the Song shows its hearers where the longing of the earlier chapters belongs: in the public covenant of marriage, celebrated by the whole community.

How the chapter makes its case. By night she seeks him whom her soul loves and cannot find him; she rises and searches the city, even asking the watchmen; then she finds him, holds him and will not let him go (vv. 1–4). Again she charges the young women not to awaken love until it pleases (v. 5). Then perfumed smoke rises from the wilderness: Solomon’s litter, guarded by sixty warriors against the terrors of the night (vv. 6–8), a carriage of cedar, silver, gold and purple, lovingly furnished (vv. 9–10). The daughters of Zion are called out to see the king crowned on his wedding day (v. 11).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need it exposes. The bride’s search echoes every believer who has sought the Lord in the dark, found him, and discovered that he holds them more firmly than they hold him. And the wedding of a son of David points beyond Solomon, of whom it was said, “his wives turned away his heart” (1 Kings 11:3), to the greater Son of David who loves one bride faithfully. The only crown men gave him was of thorns, yet he went to the cross “for the joy that was set before him” (Hebrews 12:2), and the day of the gladness of his heart is still to come: “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).

For us. When God seems far away, rise and seek him in his word, in prayer and among his people, and hold on. Honour marriage as a glad and public covenant, not a private arrangement. And look forward to the wedding that every Christian wedding announces.
3.theology:
True love seeks the beloved in his absence and holds fast when he is found (vv. 1-4); the believer seeks the Lord in seasons when he seems far (Isa 26:9). Desire must still be kept for its time (v. 5).

Marriage is a day of royal joy, and a husband protects and honours his bride (vv. 6-11). The wedding of the king points to Christ the Bridegroom (Matt 25:6), who wore a crown of thorns for the joy set before him (John 19:2; Heb 12:2) and will rejoice over his bride.
3.examples: Anyone who has reached across the bed in the dark and found no one knows the ache of these verses. And anyone who has stood on a station platform scanning the crowd for one face knows the joy of the moment that face appears.

keyVerse.quote: Go out, O daughters of Zion, and look upon King Solomon, with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, on the day of the gladness of his heart.
keyVerse.note: The chapter moves from a night of searching to this bright morning, and the verse names a wedding day as the day of the gladness of a king’s heart. It shows how highly God values marriage, and it points beyond Solomon to the Son of David whose gladness will be complete at the marriage of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7).

3.reflection:
Have you known nights when God seemed absent, like the bride on her bed (vv. 1–2)? What helps you to “rise” and seek him, rather than waiting for the feeling to pass?

“I held him, and would not let him go” (v. 4). What does it mean to hold on to Christ by faith, and how does it help to know that he holds you more firmly still?

The charge of verse 5 comes straight after a scene of intense longing. Why might the strength of desire be the very reason to guard it?

The king’s wedding is “the day of the gladness of his heart” (v. 11). How should that shape the way we celebrate and honour marriage? What does it tell you about the joy with which Christ looks forward to the marriage of the Lamb?

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love looks long, and names what it sees. On the wedding night the bridegroom praises his bride one feature at a time: eyes like doves behind her veil, hair like goats streaming down the slopes of Gilead, teeth like a flock of washed ewes, lips like a scarlet thread, cheeks like a pomegranate (vv. 1–3), a neck like David’s tower hung with shields, breasts like twin fawns (vv. 4–5). Echoing her words in 2:17, he says he will go to the mountain of myrrh until the day breaks (v. 6). Then he sums it all up: “You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you” (v. 7). This is how love sees.
verseByVerse.theology: The bridegroom's love sees the whole of his bride, and to him she is without flaw.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you are beautiful, my love, behold, you are beautiful! Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the wedding night he praises his bride slowly and in detail, because love does not glance; it gazes. He begins as in chapter 1, “you are beautiful”, and then praises her from her eyes downward, one feature at a time.

Your eyes are doves behind your veil. Glimpsed behind her veil, her eyes are doves, gentle and bright.

Like a flock of goats. To our ears, goats are not flattering. But picture a flock of black goats flowing down a far hillside, a dark wave rippling over the slope: that is her long hair as it moves. In the shepherd’s world of the Song it is high praise.

Uncertain wording. “Veil” is a rare word, which some older translations took as her locks of hair; “leaping down” is also rare. The pictures stay clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes that have come up from the washing, all of which bear twins, and not one among them has lost its young. Your lips are like a scarlet thread, and your mouth is lovely. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has noticed every feature he praises.

Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes. Her teeth are like freshly washed sheep, each with its twin: white, even and complete, none missing. In a world without dentists, that was real beauty. Her lips are a scarlet thread, her cheeks flushed like a cut pomegranate. Every line is specific; the bridegroom has paid attention.

Specific praise. Husbands can copy his method: notice, then say it. Most spouses long to hear specific praise far more often than they do. General compliments are easy; detailed delight takes attention, and attention is a form of love.

verseByVerse.quote: Your neck is like the tower of David, built in rows of stone; on it hang a thousand shields, all of them shields of warriors. Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle, that graze among the lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He praises her queenly bearing and her body, and within marriage such delight is holy.

Like the tower of David. Her neck is tall and straight, adorned with necklaces like the shields hung on David’s tower. She carries herself like a queen.

Your two breasts are like two fawns. The praise is frank and tender: fawns are soft, gentle and lovely. Scripture is not embarrassed by a husband’s delight in his wife’s body; Proverbs commands it: “rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:18). The same Bible that forbids lust outside marriage celebrates desire within it. The difference is not the body or the desire, which God made, but the marriage covenant. Inside marriage, this kind of praise is holy.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew behind “built in rows of stone” is uncertain (perhaps “built as an armoury”), but the picture of a tall, adorned tower is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: Until the day breathes and the shadows flee, I will go away to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense. You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He gathers up all his praise: through love’s eyes she is altogether beautiful.

The mountain of myrrh. He echoes her words of 2:17, “Until the day breathes and the shadows flee”. She had asked him to come to her through the night; now he will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense, fragrant heights that seem to picture his bride herself.

There is no flaw in you. Of course she had flaws; the woman of chapter 1 knew it well. But this is how a loving husband sees his wife: not blind to reality, but seeing her as a whole through the eyes of love, and delighting in the whole.

Without spot or wrinkle. Here the Song reaches toward something only the gospel makes fully true. Christ’s church is anything but flawless now, yet he gave himself for her “that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27). He has reconciled us “in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him” (Colossians 1:22). What the bridegroom says in love, Christ will one day make literally so: “there is no flaw in you”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — A Garden Locked, a Fountain Sealed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What she has kept for him alone, she gives him gladly. Calling her “my bride” for the first time, he calls her from the wild mountains of the north (v. 8). One glance of her eyes has captured his heart, and he answers her first words with his own: her love is better than wine, her kisses as sweet as milk and honey (vv. 9–11). She is a garden locked, a fountain sealed, kept for him (v. 12), and within lies a paradise of every choice fruit and spice, a well of living water (vv. 13–15). Then she speaks, calling the winds to blow on her garden and inviting him in: “Let my beloved come to his garden” (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The bride keeps herself for her husband alone, and gives herself to him freely and gladly.

verseByVerse.quote: Come with me from Lebanon, my bride; come with me from Lebanon. Depart from the peak of Amana, from the peak of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He calls his bride from wild, remote places to himself.

Come with me from Lebanon, my bride. For the first time he calls her “my bride”, as he will five times in verses 8 to 12. He calls her from the high, wild mountains of the north, Lebanon, Amana, Senir and Hermon, haunts of lions and leopards: from what is remote, dangerous and lonely, to himself.

A new life. Marriage calls a person out of the old life into a new one, as the Lord calls his people out of their old life to himself.

Uncertain wording. “Depart” may be rendered “Look” (ESV note): come down from the peaks, or gaze from them toward her new home.

verseByVerse.quote: You have captivated my heart, my sister, my bride; you have captivated my heart with one glance of your eyes, with one jewel of your necklace. How beautiful is your love, my sister, my bride! How much better is your love than wine, and the fragrance of your oils than any spice! Your lips drip nectar, my bride; honey and milk are under your tongue; the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She has captured his heart, and her love delights him as his delights her.

My sister, my bride. “Sister” is a word not of blood but of closeness: she is family to him, bound to him for life. Ancient Egyptian love songs also call the beloved “sister” and “brother” as words of tender affection. One glance, one jewel of her necklace, and his heart is captured.

How much better is your love than wine! In chapter 1 she said, “your love is better than wine” (1:2). Now he says the same to her: the love that began with her longing is fully returned.

Honey and milk are under your tongue. Milk and honey recall the promised land, “a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8). His bride is a promised land to him, sweetness and plenty.

verseByVerse.quote: A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She has kept herself for him alone, like a locked garden and a sealed spring.

A garden locked. Three pictures of one truth. Her body and her love were not open to anyone who passed by.

A fountain sealed. Proverbs uses the same pictures for faithfulness in marriage: “Drink water from your own cistern, flowing water from your own well”, and “Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth” (Proverbs 5:15, 18). The locked garden is chastity, keeping oneself sexually pure before marriage, and faithfulness within it.

Restrictive? Where the gate is left open, that sounds restrictive. The Song presents the opposite: what is given to everyone is given to no one in particular; what is kept for one can be given to him wholly. If you have not kept the gate, the gospel does not leave you locked out. Christ cleanses and restores, and the bride he presents is made pure by him. And if the gate was forced by someone else, the shame is not yours.
verseByVerse.note: The garden returns in 5:1 and 6:2, where the beloved has come into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Your shoots are an orchard of pomegranates with all choicest fruits, henna with nard, nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all trees of frankincense, myrrh and aloes, with all choice spices— a garden fountain, a well of living water, and flowing streams from Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behind the locked gate lies a paradise of every delight.

An orchard of pomegranates. Here are pomegranates and every choice fruit, and spices from across the known world: nard, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, frankincense, myrrh, aloes. No single garden could grow them all; the bride is every delight in one. And she is “a well of living water”, fresh and flowing, a spring that keeps refreshing her husband.

A well of living water. The phrase points beyond marriage. God called himself “the fountain of living waters” (Jeremiah 2:13), and Jesus promised, “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water’” (John 7:38). Without making the bride’s garden a code, Christians may rejoice that the church, filled with his Spirit, becomes a spring that refreshes others.

Uncertain wording. “Your shoots” is an unusual word, perhaps “your channels”. “Orchard” seems to come from Persian, the source of our word “paradise” (see the introduction), and some spices cannot be identified for certain.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, O north wind, and come, O south wind! Blow upon my garden, let its spices flow. Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She invites him into the garden she has kept for him, giving herself freely and gladly.

Awake, O north wind. Now the bride speaks, and her answer is the climax. She calls on the winds to carry her garden’s fragrance to him. Then comes the lovely change of pronoun: “my garden” becomes “his garden”. The locked garden is opened, freely, to the one it was kept for.

The consummation. This is the consummation of the marriage, the first union of husband and wife, told with delicacy and joy. Chastity was never meant to be a gate closed for ever; it was keeping the garden for this.

A prayer to Christ. Many Christians have also prayed these words to Christ, to whom the believer’s heart belongs. When the Spirit blows on it, the spices flow, and the fruit is his: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Can you pray the bride’s prayer, “Let my beloved come to his garden”?

4.title: You Are Altogether Beautiful, My Love
4.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 is the heart of the third poem, the wedding (3:6–5:1). The king’s procession has arrived; now the bridegroom speaks on the wedding night, and the poem reaches its climax in 4:16 and 5:1, at the centre of the whole book.

The message. In marriage a husband delights in his wife wholly, says so in detail, and sees her with love’s eyes: “there is no flaw in you.” And the love she has kept for him alone, “a garden locked”, she now gives him freely and gladly. Chastity before marriage and delight within it are not opposites: the one keeps the garden for the other.

Why it was said. Love poems that praised the beloved feature by feature were known in the ancient world, and Israel’s neighbours made sex an act of worship (see the introduction). The Song keeps such praise inside the covenant of marriage, and so teaches that the body is good, desire within marriage holy, and purity a treasure kept in order to be given.

How the chapter makes its case. He praises her from her eyes to her breasts, in pictures drawn from the flocks, the land and the city (vv. 1–5). Echoing her words in 2:17, he says he will go to the mountain of myrrh until the day breaks, and sums up: “You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you” (vv. 6–7). Calling her “my bride”, he summons her from the northern mountains (v. 8), tells her she has captured his heart, and praises her love as better than wine (vv. 9–11). She is a garden locked and a fountain sealed, an orchard of every choice fruit and spice, a well of living water (vv. 12–15). She answers by calling the winds to blow on her garden and inviting him in: “my garden” has become “his garden” (v. 16).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God revealed in him. Only one Bridegroom can say “there is no flaw in you” and make it literally true. Christ loved a church full of flaws and gave himself up for her, to present her “holy and without blemish” (Ephesians 5:27). And the bride who gives herself gladly to the one she was kept for pictures the believer whose heart belongs to Christ, a garden that by his Spirit bears fruit for him (Galatians 5:22–23).

For us. Husbands should notice, and say aloud, what they love in their wives. The unmarried should keep the garden locked for the one who will be given the key, and those who have not kept it can be made clean by Christ. Every believer may hear in “there is no flaw in you” what Christ will one day say of his whole church.
4.theology:
Delight in a spouse's body and person is good and holy within marriage (vv. 1-7; Prov 5:18-19; Heb 13:4). Chastity before marriage and faithfulness within it keep love for one person, to be given wholly and gladly (vv. 12, 16; Prov 5:15-18; 1 Cor 7:2).

The bridegroom's no flaw in you (v. 7) anticipates Christ presenting his church without spot or blemish (Eph 5:27; Col 1:22). God is the fountain of living waters, and those who believe in Christ become sources of living water and the fruit of the Spirit (vv. 15-16; John 7:38; Gal 5:22-23).
4.examples: A husband who says "you look nice" has paid a compliment; one who notices how her eyes catch the light when she laughs has paid attention, and that is what this chapter teaches. And a garden gate kept locked through years of waiting is not a loss but a gift, kept for the day it is opened gladly.

keyVerse.quote: You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you.
keyVerse.note: These words gather up all the bridegroom’s praise. Spoken by a husband, they are love’s way of seeing the whole person. Spoken by Christ of his church, they will one day be simply true, when he presents her “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27).

4.reflection:
The bridegroom praises his bride slowly and specifically (vv. 1–5). Why does specific praise mean more than general compliments? Whom could you encourage in this way this week?

“There is no flaw in you” (v. 7). How can a husband or wife say this honestly? How does Christ’s purpose to present his church “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27) change the way you see yourself and other believers?

The bride is “a garden locked” (v. 12) until she opens it gladly to her husband (v. 16). How does this picture answer the claim that the Bible’s sexual ethics are merely restrictive? What does the gospel say to those who have not kept the gate?

Many Christians have prayed, “Let my beloved come to his garden” (v. 16). What would it mean to offer your life to Christ in this way, and what fruit would you long for him to find?
