verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wedding night is a feast, and God’s word blesses it. The bridegroom answers the invitation she gave at the end of chapter 4 (4:16) and comes to his garden. Everything she kept for him is now his, and he receives it with joy: myrrh and spice, honeycomb and honey, wine and milk. Then a voice stands back and speaks over the couple: “Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!” This one verse closes the first half of the Song. Married love, given and received within the covenant of marriage, is not a concession God reluctantly allows but a gift he spreads like a table and invites his people to enjoy.
verseByVerse.theology: The consummation of marriage is received as a feast, and blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: I came to my garden, my sister, my bride, I gathered my myrrh with my spice, I ate my honeycomb with my honey, I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bridegroom comes into the garden she offered him, and a voice blesses their union: married love is a feast to be enjoyed.

I came to my garden. At the end of chapter 4 the bride said, “Let my beloved come to his garden” (4:16). Here is his answer, and every line is “my”: my myrrh, my honeycomb, my wine. What she kept for him is now his, and he receives it with delight. The poem tells the wedding night with great restraint and great joy.

Eat, friends, drink. A voice, the guests’ or the poet’s, blesses them: this is good; enjoy it fully. Scripture forbids drunkenness with wine (Ephesians 5:18); here it urges a husband and wife to be overcome with love for each other, as Proverbs does: “be intoxicated always in her love” (Proverbs 5:19).

A feast, not a concession. The church has sometimes spoken of sex in marriage as if it were only allowed. Verse 1 calls it a feast, and blesses it. Scripture’s own story ends at a wedding meal (Revelation 19:9), and no one who belongs to Christ, married or single, is left out of that one.

Uncertain wording. The last word of the verse (dodim) can mean “love”, as in the ESV, or “lovers”, so the line may address the couple themselves: drink deeply, O lovers. Either way, it blesses the union.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love that is slow to answer can find the beloved gone, and must then go out at cost to seek him. Half asleep, the bride hears her beloved knocking and calling her by four tender names (v. 2), but she makes small excuses (v. 3). His hand at the latch stirs her heart, and she rises at last, only to find him gone (vv. 4–6). Searching the city, she is beaten by the watchmen (v. 7), yet her love holds: she charges the daughters of Jerusalem to tell him she is sick with love (v. 8). It is the most painful scene in the Song, and the most honest about ordinary married life, and about our slowness towards Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: Even real love can grow slow to respond, and the cost of delay is felt in the beloved's absence.

verseByVerse.quote: I slept, but my heart was awake. A sound! My beloved is knocking. "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, for my head is wet with dew, my locks with the drops of the night."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the night her husband comes home wet with dew and asks tenderly to be let in, while she is half asleep. A new scene opens the Song’s second half, and it is a painful one.

Open to me. She is drowsing, perhaps dreaming, as in 3:1–4. He calls her by four names of love, my sister, my love, my dove, my perfect one, wanting to come in to her. His hair is soaked with dew; nothing in his words is harsh or demanding.

Christ at the door. The picture of a beloved knocking has entered Christian devotion through the words of the risen Christ to a lukewarm church: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). Puritans such as Richard Sibbes heard Christ knocking at a drowsy church here too. That is a true echo (see the introduction), so long as the scene is first heard as what it is, a marriage.

Is it wrong for a spouse to refuse? Tiredness and hard seasons happen, and he does not force or demand. But habitual refusal harms a marriage: spouses are to give themselves to each other and “not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time” (1 Corinthians 7:5). That is a call to generous love on both sides, never a licence to pressure: love that forces is not the love this book sings.

verseByVerse.quote: I had put off my garment; how could I put it on? I had bathed my feet; how could I soil them? My beloved put his hand to the latch, and my heart was thrilled within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her love is real and her excuses are small, but a stirred heart is not yet an opened door.

How could I put it on? She has undressed and washed her feet for the night. She is not refusing him, just not bothered enough, just now, to get up.

The slow drift. Every married person knows this: not rejection but the slow drift of comfort, tiredness and self-concern that leaves a spouse knocking. Most marriages that cool do not end in a great quarrel. They end in a long series of doors not opened.

My heart was thrilled within me. He tries the latch, and her heart leaps. She does love him, but feeling alone has not yet got her out of bed.

The same drift in faith. Christ calls through his word, a stirring of conscience, a chance to pray or serve, and we stay put. Jesus told his disciples to be ready to “open the door to him at once when he comes and knocks” (Luke 12:36), and in Gethsemane they slept: “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41). None of us has always answered at once. He did, always doing what pleased his Father, and in him our slowness is forgiven; the Spirit who stirred her heart stirs ours to rise and open.

verseByVerse.quote: I arose to open to my beloved, and my hands dripped with myrrh, my fingers with liquid myrrh, on the handles of the bolt. I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had turned and gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but found him not; I called him, but he gave no answer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When at last she opens, he is gone, and she searches and calls in vain: delay in love has a cost.

My hands dripped with myrrh. On the bolt she finds liquid myrrh, his token or her own perfume put on for him. The door is fragrant with love, and he is gone.

Delay has a cost. He is not sulking. He did not break the door down, and he did not wait forever: opportunities for love do not stay open indefinitely.

When the Lord seems withdrawn. Believers can lose the sense of the Lord’s nearness, sometimes after being slow to respond. The psalmist prayed then, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Psalm 51:12). The Lord does not abandon his own, but he may let us feel the absence we chose so that we learn to seek him. And the promise stands: “You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart” (Jeremiah 29:13).

Not every darkness is a rebuke. Not every dark season follows delay; Job knew darkness he had not caused. If heaviness lingers, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor and see a doctor too: medicine is no failure of faith.

Uncertain wording. “My soul failed me when he spoke” is literally my soul went out when he spoke: his remembered words grieve her. Some take the verb as “turn away”, at his leaving. Either way, love woke too late.

verseByVerse.quote: The watchmen found me as they went about in the city; they beat me, they bruised me, they took away my veil, those watchmen of the walls. I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him I am sick with love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Searching at night, she is beaten by the watchmen, yet her love does not turn bitter: she is still sick with love for him.

They beat me, they bruised me. In chapter 3 the watchmen let her pass (3:3). This time they beat her and take away her veil. The Song does not say why; those who should protect do not always do so.

I am sick with love. Bruised, she is not bitter. The words she used in 2:5 in the joy of his presence she now uses in the pain of his absence. Real love, and real faith, longs for the beloved as much in his absence as in his presence. “Though you have not seen him, you love him” (1 Peter 1:8).

Does the Song approve the beating? No. It reports a wrong, as Scripture reports many, without blaming her. Nothing here excuses violence against a woman, in the street or in a home; anyone being hurt should seek safety at once.

Uncertain wording. The word for “veil” is rare (elsewhere only in Isaiah 3:23) and may be a wide shawl or mantle rather than a face veil. Taking it shamed as well as hurt her.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Asked why her beloved is worth such a search, the bride answers with delight, and her delight is her testimony. The daughters of Jerusalem put the question twice: what is he more than any other (v. 9)? She does not argue. She paints him from head to foot: radiant and ruddy, a head of gold, eyes like doves, fragrant cheeks and lips, arms, body and legs like the gold, ivory and precious stone of a royal statue, his bearing like the cedars of Lebanon (vv. 10–15). Then she gathers it up: he is “altogether desirable”, her beloved and her friend (v. 16). The only full portrait of him in the Song is drawn while he is absent, by a bride who has just been slow to open to him.
verseByVerse.theology: When asked what makes her beloved different, the bride can describe him in detail, and her delight is her testimony.

verseByVerse.quote: What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you thus adjure us?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The daughters of Jerusalem ask what makes her beloved better than any other, and their question opens the way for her praise.

What is your beloved more than another beloved? They ask it twice: every woman has a beloved; what makes yours worth such a search?

The world’s question. It is the question the world asks the church. You speak of Jesus as if he were more than any other teacher, any other hope, any other love: why? Her answer is the model for ours, and it works: by 6:1 the same women are asking where he has gone, “that we may seek him with you”. Delighted praise draws people as argument alone seldom does.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved is radiant and ruddy, distinguished among ten thousand. His head is the finest gold; his locks are wavy, black as a raven. His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, bathed in milk, sitting beside a full pool.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She does not argue for her beloved; she describes him, beginning with a face that stands out in any crowd.

Radiant and ruddy. Glowing with health and life. The same pair describes Jerusalem’s princes in better days, “whiter than milk” and “more ruddy than coral” (Lamentations 4:7), and young David was “ruddy” and handsome (1 Samuel 16:12). Distinguished among ten thousand: you could pick him out of any crowd.

His head is the finest gold. Her praise moves downward, as his did in chapter 4: a head of finest gold, thick hair black as a raven. He had said her eyes were doves (4:1); she says the same of his, gentle and bright, the whites clear as if bathed in milk.

Uncertain wording. Wavy is a rare word, perhaps curled like palm fronds; “sitting beside a full pool” is literally sitting upon fullness: doves by brimming water, or eyes set like jewels. The picture is plain either way.

verseByVerse.quote: His cheeks are like beds of spices, mounds of sweet-smelling herbs. His lips are lilies, dripping liquid myrrh. His arms are rods of gold, set with jewels. His body is polished ivory, bedecked with sapphires. His legs are alabaster columns, set on bases of gold. His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From face to feet she pictures him as a royal statue of gold, ivory and precious stone, fragrant and strong, splendid all through.

His cheeks are like beds of spices. His face is fragrant, and his lips, dripping myrrh, make his kisses and words as lovely as his looks. Then his strength: arms like golden rods, a body of polished ivory, legs like alabaster pillars, his bearing tall as Lebanon’s cedars. She describes a precious statue, splendid from head to foot.

Describing our Lord. A Christian reading this cannot help asking: could I describe my Lord with half this delight? Scripture gives us far more to say than she had. He is “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature” (Hebrews 1:3) and “the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15), the king of whom the psalm sings, “grace is poured upon your lips” (Psalm 45:2). Many can explain doctrines about Christ; few can describe him with this love. Watch him in the Gospels, how he spoke, whom he touched, how he died, and tell someone what you saw.

Uncertain wording. “Sapphires” is probably lapis lazuli; the “jewels” (tarshish) may be topaz or beryl; “body” is literally belly, the trunk. The picture, precious and solid, is clear.

verseByVerse.quote: His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She sums him up: everything about him is delightful, and he is both her beloved and her friend.

His mouth is most sweet. The word is in Hebrew “palate”: his kisses and his words are sweetness itself. As he called her “altogether beautiful” (4:7), she calls him “altogether desirable”.

This is my beloved and this is my friend. Her final words are the simplest and perhaps the deepest. The best marriages are both: friendship carries a marriage when passion ebbs.

Bridegroom and friend. Jesus offers his people the same double gift. He is the Bridegroom (Mark 2:19), and he says, “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). Yet he came with “no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2): the altogether desirable one was despised, so that people who saw nothing in him might be won. Paul counted everything loss “because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord” (Philippians 3:8). Can you say of him, “This is my beloved and this is my friend”?

5.title: This Is My Beloved and This Is My Friend
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 stands at the centre of the Song. The bride, “A garden locked” (4:12), has invited her beloved in (4:16); verse 1 is his answer and closes the wedding section, and verse 2 opens the second half of the book, where love is tested.

The message. Married love is God’s good feast, and it still has to be tended. Even a bride who truly loves can be slow to open, and slowness costs; but loss need not end love. Pressed to say why her beloved is worth the search, she pours out praise and comes to rest where every lasting love rests: “This is my beloved and this is my friend” (v. 16).

Why it was said. The Song is wisdom about love (see the introduction), and wisdom knows that love does not keep itself. So the poem does not stop at the wedding night. It goes on into the ordinary nights after, where comfort, tiredness and self-concern can leave a spouse knocking, and it shows a love that recovers.

How the chapter makes its case. First the feast [v. 1]: he comes to his garden, and a voice blesses the couple, “Eat, friends, drink, and be drunk with love!” Then the slow door [vv. 2–8]: he knocks in the night, wet with dew, calling her by four names of love; she makes small excuses, rises too late and finds him gone; searching the city, she is beaten by the watchmen, yet still sends word that she is sick with love. Last the portrait [vv. 9–16]: asked what makes him different, she answers not with argument but with description, from his golden head to his cedar-like bearing, and ends with friendship.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the need the chapter exposes. The bride was slow to open; Christ never was. The risen Lord still stands knocking at the door of a lukewarm church (Revelation 3:20), and in Gethsemane, while his friends slept, he stayed awake and went out into the night for them. Her beloved is “distinguished among ten thousand”; Christ came with “no beauty that we should desire him” (Isaiah 53:2), despised so that people who once saw nothing in him might come to call him altogether desirable, their Bridegroom and their friend (John 15:15).

For us. Husbands and wives: watch for the slow drift, and open the door. Every believer: when Christ knocks through his word, do not wait until the moment has passed; his welcome is still there for the one who comes late. And when someone asks what is so special about him, try what the bride did: before you argue, describe him.
5.theology:
The consummation of marriage is a blessed feast (v. 1; Heb 13:4). Love must be tended; slowness to respond, even without hostility, has real costs (vv. 2-6; Luke 12:36), and those who have drifted are called to seek again with the whole heart (Jer 29:13; Ps 51:12).

Love is shown by delight in the beloved and by the ability to describe him (vv. 10-16). Christ is the radiance of God's glory (Heb 1:3), altogether desirable to those who know him (Phil 3:8), and both Bridegroom and friend (John 15:15).
5.examples: Ask a widow about the husband she lost, and she will not give you a list of his opinions; her face changes and she describes him. That is what the bride does when the world asks, "What is your beloved more than another?", and it is what the church is asked to do for Christ.

keyVerse.quote: His mouth is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable. This is my beloved and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.
keyVerse.note: The chapter turns on this sentence. After a night of slowness and loss, the bride does not complain about her beloved; asked what makes him special, she praises him until words run out, then calls him her friend. It is what the church is to say of Christ: not only that he is true, but that he is altogether desirable, and ours.

5.reflection:
Verse 1 blesses married love as a feast. Why do you think Christians have sometimes found it hard to speak of sex in marriage as God’s good gift? How might this verse help a church speak of it with both joy and care?

The bride’s excuses in verse 3 are small, yet they cost her dearly. What small excuses most often leave a husband or wife, a friend, or the Lord knocking in your life? What would opening the door look like this week?

In verses 5–8 she seeks her beloved through pain and still says she is sick with love. How do you respond when God seems far away? What helps you keep seeking him (Jeremiah 29:13), and whom could you ask for help?

Asked what makes her beloved special (v. 9), the bride describes him (vv. 10–16). If a friend asked you what is so special about Jesus, what would you say about him, not only about what he has done for you?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — Where Has Your Beloved Gone?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The bride’s delight in her beloved draws others to seek him, and in his absence she rests in belonging to him. The daughters of Jerusalem, who asked what made him special (5:9), now ask where he has gone, “that we may seek him with you” (v. 1). She knows the answer: he has gone down to his garden, the place of their love, which is herself (v. 2). Then the refrain of belonging returns, turned round from 2:16 so that his claim on her comes first: “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine” (v. 3). After the night of loss she leans not on her hold on him but on his hold on her.
verseByVerse.theology: The bride's delight in her beloved makes others want to seek him, and in his absence she rests in belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Where has your beloved turned, that we may seek him with you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bride’s praise has worked: the women who doubted now want to find her beloved with her.

Where has your beloved gone? In 5:9 the daughters of Jerusalem asked, with some doubt, what made him special. Now they are asking not why but where, and they want to seek him “with you”. Her description has made them want him too.

How people are drawn to Christ. That is how people are usually drawn to Christ: not by argument first, but by hearing someone who loves him describe him. So the woman at the well brought her town: “Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did” (John 4:29). When believers speak of their Lord with delight, others begin to ask where he may be found.

verseByVerse.quote: My beloved has gone down to his garden to the beds of spices, to graze in the gardens and to gather lilies. I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She knows where he is, with her, and she rests not in her grip on him but in his claim on her.

Gone down to his garden. In chapter 5 she searched the city in vain. Now she answers without hesitation: in his garden. In the Song the garden is the bride herself (4:12, 16; 5:1); he has gone where he belongs, to her. To graze may be rendered “to pasture his flock” (ESV note): the shepherd is among his lilies.

I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine. The words of 2:16 return, reversed. There she said, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” Now, after the night of loss, she begins with his claim on her. When she felt least sure of her grip on him, she rested in his grip on her.

In a season of dryness. That is the believer’s comfort when faith feels dry. Feelings of nearness come and go; his covenant promise does not. Jesus said, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37), and of his sheep, “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–10 — My Dove, My Perfect One, Is the Only One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He comes back without a word of reproach, and his love is the same as before. He calls her as lovely as two great cities and as awesome as an army with banners (v. 4), then repeats, almost word for word, the praise of their wedding night (vv. 5–7; compare 4:1–3): her slowness has not changed how he sees her. In a palace full of queens and concubines she is “the only one” (vv. 8–9), and the other women, instead of resenting her, praise her as dawn, moon and sun (v. 10). Restored love does not demote the one it forgives; it makes her shine.
verseByVerse.theology: Love restored speaks the same words it spoke before, and to the husband his wife is the only one.

verseByVerse.quote: You are beautiful as Tirzah, my love, lovely as Jerusalem, awesome as an army with banners.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He returns with no word of reproach, only praise: she is as lovely as a royal city and as majestic as an army.

Beautiful as Tirzah. After the closed door we might expect reproach. There is none. Tirzah was a city famous for its beauty and for a time a royal capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:23), and Jerusalem was the city of God.

Awesome as an army with banners. Her beauty is not only gentle but majestic, like a great army marching with its standards raised. A husband who loves his wife is not only charmed by her. He is in awe of her.

Uncertain wording. “An army with banners” translates one Hebrew word, something like bannered ones. It may mean troops marching under their standards or, since the phrase returns in verse 10 beside dawn, moon and sun, the starry hosts of heaven.
verseByVerse.note: Tirzah (its name suggests "pleasing") later served as an early capital of the northern kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn away your eyes from me, for they overwhelm me— Your hair is like a flock of goats leaping down the slopes of Gilead. Your teeth are like a flock of ewes that have come up from the washing; all of them bear twins; not one among them has lost its young. Your cheeks are like halves of a pomegranate behind your veil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He repeats the very praise of their wedding night: her slowness has not changed how he sees her.

Turn away your eyes from me. Her eyes overwhelm him, as in 4:9. And these lines are almost exactly the words he spoke in 4:1–3, before the door was left closed. He does not compose new, cooler praise.

What forgiveness looks like. That is forgiveness in a marriage: not “I will love you again when you have earned it”, but the same words, the same delight, restored. And it is how Christ restores his people. After Peter denied him, “the Lord turned and looked at Peter”, and Peter “went out and wept bitterly” (Luke 22:61–62). But the risen Lord did not give Peter a lesser place. Three times he asked him, “do you love me?”, and three times gave him back his calling (John 21:15–17).

What it does not mean. Forgiving is not pretending nothing happened, and it never means returning to danger: where there has been abuse, safety comes first, and trust is rebuilt slowly, with help. The Song pictures a small failure in a good marriage, met with generous love.

verseByVerse.quote: There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and virgins without number. My dove, my perfect one, is the only one, the only one of her mother, pure to her who bore her. The young women saw her and called her blessed; the queens and concubines also, and they praised her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Among all the women a king could have, she is the one: love as God designed it is one man and one woman, each the only one to the other.

The only one. A king’s palace was full of women. And yet, twice: “the only one”. That is the shape of love as God designed it: “they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). The Song lifts up this ideal even though the kings of Israel, Solomon among them, so often fell short of it.

Sixty queens and eighty concubines. Concubines were wives of lower rank. These numbers are far fewer than the 700 wives and 300 concubines of 1 Kings 11:3, perhaps because the Song comes from earlier in Solomon’s reign, or because the numbers are poetic. Does the Bible approve of such a harem? No. It records polygamy without commending it, the law forbade the king to multiply wives (Deuteronomy 17:17), and Solomon’s wives turned his heart away (1 Kings 11:4). The Song itself sets the one beloved above them all.

They praised her. The other women do not resent her; they praise her. Christians have seen in this a picture of the church, loved by Christ as his only bride, whose good life even a hostile world sometimes cannot help admiring (1 Peter 2:12).

Uncertain wording. “Pure” can also mean “chosen” or “favourite”: she may be her mother’s darling as well as her husband’s only one. The same word returns in verse 10 as “bright”.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is this who looks down like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, bright as the sun, awesome as an army with banners?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The women reach for the largest pictures they have: the bride once ashamed of her darkness now shines like dawn, moon and sun.

Who is this who looks down like the dawn? These seem to be the words of the queens and young women, the praise verse 9 promised, and they take her beauty to the sky.

Bright as the sun. In chapter 1 she said, “Do not gaze at me because I am dark” (1:6). Now she is “bright as the sun”. That is what love has done for her. A bride who is truly loved begins to shine. And Jesus promised that “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love takes the bride by surprise and lifts her up, and everyone wants to see her. She went down to the nut orchard to see whether spring had come (v. 11), and before she knew it her desire had set her among royal chariots (v. 12), a verse whose wording is among the hardest in the Song. Then others call to her four times, “Return, return, O Shulammite”, and for the first time the bride is given a name (v. 13). The woman who once asked not to be stared at (1:6) is now the one everyone longs to look at, and the scene opens on a dance that the next chapter describes.
verseByVerse.theology: The bride is named, called back and admired; love's joy draws others to see it.

verseByVerse.quote: I went down to the nut orchard to look at the blossoms of the valley, to see whether the vines had budded, whether the pomegranates were in bloom. Before I was aware, my desire set me among the chariots of my kinsman, a prince.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love takes her by surprise and lifts her up before she knows it.

I went down to the nut orchard. Spring in the Song is the season of love (2:11–13), and the garden is the place of love: budding vines, pomegranates in bloom. Someone, probably the bride, goes to see whether love is in flower.

My desire set me among the chariots. The general sense seems to be that her desire carried her into a place of honour, as if swept up into a royal chariot beside her prince.

Uncertain wording. Verse 12 is one of the hardest in the Song, and no one should be too sure of its meaning. Word for word it runs something like I did not know; my soul set me chariots of my-people-noble. The last words may be a name, “chariots of Ammi-Nadib” (ESV note), or mean “my noble people”, or, as the ESV takes them, “my kinsman, a prince”. Ancient translations differ too.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, return, O Shulammite, return, return, that we may look upon you. Why should you look upon the Shulammite, as upon a dance before two armies?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone calls the bride back to look at her, and for the first time she is given a name: the Shulammite.

Return, return, O Shulammite. The others call her back four times because they want to see her. The name is probably a feminine form matching Solomon’s own (Shelomoh), something like “the Solomon woman”; if so, even her title ties her to her beloved.

As upon a dance before two armies. Someone answers, perhaps the bride, perhaps the bridegroom: why gaze on her like this? It seems to picture a festive dance that draws every eye, and the next chapter begins his praise of her as she dances.

Return, return. The woman who did not want to be looked at (1:6) is now the one everyone wants to see. Christians have borrowed this chorus as a call to anyone who has wandered: come back, so that we may see you among us again. The Lord’s own call is warmer still: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Malachi 3:7).

Uncertain wording. The meaning of “Shulammite” is not certain. Besides the link with Solomon’s name, some connect it with the village of Shunem, home of Abishag (1 Kings 1:3), and others with the word for peace or wholeness, “the perfect one”. “Two armies” may be a place name, “dance of Mahanaim” (ESV note), the town whose name means two camps (Genesis 32:2).
verseByVerse.note: Song 6:13 is 7:1 in Hebrew (ESV note). “Shulammite” may mean “the perfect one” or be a feminine echo of Solomon’s name.

6.title: I Am My Beloved's and My Beloved Is Mine
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 follows straight on from the night of loss (5:2–8) and the bride’s portrait of her absent beloved (5:10–16). The daughters of Jerusalem asked what made him special; now they want to find him too. The chapter completes the section that began at 5:2 and opens the restoration that runs into chapter 7.

The message. Love that has been tested comes back not cooler but surer. In his absence the bride rests in belonging to him; when he returns, he greets her without a word of reproach, speaks the same praise as before and calls her “the only one” (v. 9). Real love restores; it does not demote.

Why it was said. The Song was sung in a royal world of “sixty queens and eighty concubines” (v. 8), and Solomon’s own story shows where that led (see the introduction). Against it the Song holds up one man and one woman, each the only one to the other, and a love that survives failure without keeping score.

How the chapter makes its case. Her praise draws the daughters to seek him with her, and she knows where he is: in his garden, which is herself; she rests in his claim on her, “I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine” [vv. 1–3]. He speaks: she is majestic as a royal city and an army with banners, and he repeats his wedding-night praise almost word for word; among all the palace women she is the only one, and even they praise her [vv. 4–10]. The chapter ends with love lifting her up before she knows it, and with others calling the Shulammite back so that they may look at her [vv. 11–13].

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The bridegroom who returns without reproach is a picture of the Lord who “turned and looked at Peter” (Luke 22:61) and after the resurrection gave him back his calling (John 21:15–17). The bride’s rest in his claim on her answers to the covenant promise Christ keeps: “All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). And the church he loves as his one bride will one day shine, as the bride shines here (v. 10; Matthew 13:43).

For us. When you cannot feel that Christ is yours, rest in the truth that you are his. When you have failed him, expect not a lesser place but the same love. And in marriage, forgive the way he does: say the same loving words again, without the cooler edge.
6.theology:
Delight in the beloved draws others to seek him (v. 1); the church's love for Christ is part of its witness. In seasons of absence, the believer rests in belonging to the Lord (v. 3; John 6:37).

Love restored speaks the same words as before; forgiveness does not give the forgiven a lower place (vv. 5-7; Luke 22:61-62). God's design for marriage is one man and one woman, each the only one to the other (vv. 8-9; Gen 2:24). The loved bride shines (v. 10), as Christ's church will.
6.examples: After a quarrel, a husband who says the same loving words he said the week before, without a cooler edge, has shown what forgiveness is. And on the days when you cannot feel that Christ is yours, you can still rest in the fact that you are his.

keyVerse.quote: I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine; he grazes among the lilies.
keyVerse.note: The refrain of belonging returns after the night of loss, but turned round: her first thought is now his claim on her, not hers on him. That is where every tested believer learns to rest. Feelings of nearness come and go, but Christ’s hold on his people does not loosen.

6.reflection:
In 5:9 the daughters of Jerusalem doubted; in 6:1 they want to seek him with her. What changed them? Who first made Christ attractive to you, and how?

In 2:16 the bride said, “My beloved is mine, and I am his”; in 6:3 she puts his claim first. Why does that order matter in seasons when faith feels dry (John 10:28)?

After her failure he repeats the same praise as before (vv. 5–7; compare 4:1–3). What does real forgiveness look like in a marriage or a friendship, and what does it not mean? How did Jesus show it to Peter (John 21:15–17)?

Among many, she is “the only one” (v. 9). How can a husband or wife show the other that they are the only one? How does Christ’s love for his church as his one bride encourage you?

7.text: <sup>1</sup>How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand.<sup>2</sup>Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies.<sup>3</sup>Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.<sup>4</sup>Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus.<sup>5</sup>Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.<sup>6</sup>How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights!<sup>7</sup>Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters.<sup>8</sup>I say I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. Oh may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples,<sup>9</sup>and your mouth like the best wine. It goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over lips and teeth.<sup>10</sup>I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.<sup>11</sup>Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and lodge in the villages;<sup>12</sup>let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.<sup>13</sup>The mandrakes give forth fragrance, and beside our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — How Beautiful and Pleasant You Are
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A husband’s delight in his own wife’s body, spoken openly, specifically and to her alone, is a holy thing. Watching her dance (6:13), he praises her from her feet upward: graceful feet, a body like the work of a master craftsman, a feast of wine and wheat (vv. 1–2); then fawns, an ivory tower, calm pools, a noble profile, a head carried like Mount Carmel, and hair that holds a king captive (vv. 3–5). He gathers it up, “How beautiful and pleasant you are” (v. 6), likens her to a tall date palm and resolves to climb it (vv. 7–8). Her kiss is the best wine, and as he speaks, she takes up his words (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Delight in one's own spouse, spoken openly and specifically, is a gift of God and a duty of love.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful are your feet in sandals, O noble daughter! Your rounded thighs are like jewels, the work of a master hand. Your navel is a rounded bowl that never lacks mixed wine. Your belly is a heap of wheat, encircled with lilies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Watching her dance, he praises her from her feet upward as the work of a master craftsman and a feast to him.

How beautiful are your feet in sandals. In chapter 4 he praised her from her eyes downward. Here he begins at her feet, apparently watching the dance of 6:13. He calls her “O noble daughter”, a word of honour: the vineyard girl of chapter 1 is treated as royalty.

The work of a master hand. Her body is craftsmanship, and someone made it. That is a quiet act of worship. The psalmist says the same of himself: “I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made” (Psalm 139:14). To delight in a wife’s body is to admire the Creator’s work.

Wine and wheat. A bowl of wine and a heap of wheat, the two staples of a feast: she is nourishment and celebration to him. The farm images are meant warmly: abundance, harvest.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “navel” is rare, and some think it refers more intimately to her body. The Song speaks with veiled restraint, and the exact reference is uncertain; the sense of beauty and plenty is plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Your two breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle. Your neck is like an ivory tower. Your eyes are pools in Heshbon, by the gate of Bath-rabbim. Your nose is like a tower of Lebanon, which looks toward Damascus. Your head crowns you like Carmel, and your flowing locks are like purple; a king is held captive in the tresses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He names her beauty feature by feature, up to the hair that holds a king captive, because love that is awake pays attention.

Your neck is like an ivory tower. He repeats the picture of 4:5 and adds new ones. Her neck is an ivory tower, pale and stately. Her eyes are calm pools by the city gate, where people lingered. Her nose is like a watchtower: a strange compliment to us, but high praise in a world that prized a strong profile.

A king is held captive in the tresses. Her head is carried like Carmel, the ridge rising green above the sea. Her hair is dark and lustrous as royal purple, and in it the king is a prisoner. He has an army and a throne, and he is captured by his wife’s hair, and glad of it. Many husbands and wives think kind things they never say; the Song gives permission, and an example, to say them.

Uncertain wording. Heshbon was a town east of the Jordan; its pools were evidently well known, but “Bath-rabbim” (daughter of many) is otherwise unknown, perhaps one of its gates. The word for “tresses” is rare too; elsewhere it means watering troughs, so the king may be pictured caught as in running water.

verseByVerse.quote: How beautiful and pleasant you are, O loved one, with all your delights! Your stature is like a palm tree, and your breasts are like its clusters.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sums her up as both beautiful and pleasant, tall and graceful as a date palm.

How beautiful and pleasant you are. She is lovely to look at and lovely to be with. Beauty without pleasantness soon wears thin, and pleasantness makes beauty last.

Your stature is like a palm tree. She is tall and graceful as a date palm, the tree of the oasis: shade, sweetness and life in a dry land, and her breasts are like its clusters of fruit.

Uncertain wording. “With all your delights” may be rendered “among delights” (ESV note): she is the delight of all delights.

verseByVerse.quote: I say I will climb the palm tree and lay hold of its fruit. Oh may your breasts be like clusters of the vine, and the scent of your breath like apples, and your mouth like the best wine. It goes down smoothly for my beloved, gliding over lips and teeth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His desire is frank, and it is all for his own wife; and she answers him in his own words.

I will climb the palm tree. Having compared her to a palm, he says he will climb it. The Song does not pretend that desire is polite. It is frank, and it is directed entirely to his own wife. That is the point. The same Bible that says “everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28) gives a husband these words for his own bride. Lust takes from anyone; this desire is for one person, within a covenant, and delights to give.

For my beloved. Then the speaker seems to change. In the middle of his praise she answers, taking his words into her own mouth: the wine goes down smoothly “for my beloved”. They are no longer two voices taking turns. They finish each other’s lines.

Textual note. The last clause is difficult: the ancient Greek, Syriac and Latin translations read as the ESV does, while the Hebrew reads “causing the lips of sleepers to speak” (ESV note). Either way her kiss is like the best wine, and it is his.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — Come, My Beloved, Let Us Go Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Mature love rests in being desired, and freely gives itself. The refrain sounds for the last time, in its deepest form: “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me” (v. 10). The word for desire is the one used in the curse of Genesis 3:16, and here love is restored. Resting in his love, she takes the initiative: she invites him out to the fields and villages, early to the vineyards to see the spring, and there she will give him her love (vv. 11–12). She has laid up choice fruits for him, new as well as old (v. 13), the treasures of a marriage that has lasted.
verseByVerse.theology: Mature love rests in being desired and takes the initiative in giving itself.

verseByVerse.quote: I am my beloved's, and his desire is for me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The bride rests in the settled knowledge that her husband wants her: love has grown from claiming to resting.

The refrain for the last time. The refrain comes for the third time, changed again. In 2:16 she said, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” In 6:3, after the night she lost him, she began with belonging to him. Now she says only that half, and adds something new: “his desire is for me”.

Desire restored. The Hebrew word for desire is rare, found elsewhere only in Genesis 3:16 and 4:7. After the fall, “Your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Genesis 3:16): desire became part of a struggle for control, answered by harsh rule (see the note there). Here desire runs the other way, his for her, and it is love, not mastery. Here is love as it was meant to be, which Christ came to restore.

Where mature love arrives. Not “he is mine”, asserting a claim; not even “I am his”, stating a duty; but resting in the settled knowledge that he wants her. A wife who knows her husband desires her, and a husband who knows his wife delights in him, can weather a great deal.

The soul with God. And it is where the soul arrives with God. The believer’s peace is not finally in the strength of his grip on Christ, but in knowing that Christ desires him. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). “As the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). Can you say it: his desire is for me?

For the single and the widowed. For the single, the widowed, or anyone who has never heard a human voice say this, that comfort is not second best. Christ’s desire is for every one of his people, married or not, and it does not fade.
verseByVerse.note: “Desire” is the same Hebrew word as in Genesis 3:16; there it marks conflict after the fall, here love restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, my beloved, let us go out into the fields and lodge in the villages; let us go out early to the vineyards and see whether the vines have budded, whether the grape blossoms have opened and the pomegranates are in bloom. There I will give you my love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Secure in his love, she takes the lead and plans a time away, where she will give him her love.

Come, my beloved. Now she takes the initiative. In chapter 2 he said, “Arise, my love, my beautiful one, and come away” (2:10). Now she says it to him: out early to the vineyards to see the spring, away from the house and the work.

There I will give you my love. Desire in marriage is not only the husband’s to express, and it is always given, never demanded or forced. Paul says as much: “The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband” (1 Corinthians 7:3).

Making occasions for love. Love also needs occasions made for it. Marriages are kept alive by such plans: the evening kept free, the walk, the weekend away. Waiting for love to happen is often how it stops happening.

Uncertain wording. “In the villages” may be rendered “among the henna plants” (ESV note); the Hebrew can be read either way. Either way, she wants him to herself.

verseByVerse.quote: The mandrakes give forth fragrance, and beside our doors are all choice fruits, new as well as old, which I have laid up for you, O my beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She has stored up delights for him, new and old: a lasting marriage keeps treasures of both kinds.

The mandrakes give forth fragrance. Mandrakes were associated with love and fertility; Rachel and Leah once bargained over them (Genesis 30:14–16). Their scent says the season of love has come.

New as well as old. Then the loveliest phrase. A marriage that lasts has both: new joys, and the treasured old ones, the remembered early days, the family jokes, the hard years survived together. Nothing is wasted; everything is laid up for the beloved.

In your marriage, and before the Lord. What have you laid up for your husband or wife, and when did you last bring it out? And what have you laid up for the Lord, who receives every act of love done in his name, new and old alike?
verseByVerse.note: The mandrake is a low plant whose small yellow fruit has a strong, sweet scent.

7.title: His Desire Is for Me
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 7 continues the restoration that began in 6:4. Others have called the Shulammite back to watch her dance (6:13); now her husband praises her, and she answers with the last and deepest form of the Song’s refrain before inviting him away into the spring.

The message. A husband’s delight in his wife’s body, spoken openly and directed to her alone, is holy; and a wife may rest in being wanted and may take the lead in love. The chapter turns on one short line, “I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me” (v. 10): love has grown from claiming to resting.

Why it was said. In a world where a king could keep “sixty queens and eighty concubines” (6:8), and desire was easily turned into possession or lust, the Song shows desire as God meant it: frank, specific and faithful (see the introduction). And the word “desire” in verse 10 was last heard in the curse of Genesis 3:16; here it speaks of love restored.

How the chapter makes its case. He praises her from her feet upward as he watches her dance: the work of a master hand, a feast of wine and wheat, a head carried like Mount Carmel, hair in which a king is held captive [vv. 1–5]. He sums her up as beautiful and pleasant, tall as a palm whose fruit he will climb to take; her kiss is the best wine, and as he speaks she takes up his words [vv. 6–9]. Then she speaks: “his desire is for me”; she invites him out to the vineyards, where she will give him her love, and shows him the choice fruits she has laid up, new as well as old [vv. 10–13].

Where it leads. To Christ, by pattern and by the character of God revealed in him. The desire that went wrong in Eden is glimpsed here as it was meant to be, a love Christ came to restore. Above all, the bride’s rest in being desired is the believer’s rest in God: “as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you” (Isaiah 62:5). Christ’s desire for his people is not a passing mood but a covenant love that went to the cross, and “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

For us. Husbands and wives: notice each other and say what you see, make occasions for love, and give rather than demand. Every believer, married or single: your peace does not rest on the strength of your hold on Christ, but on his desire for you, which does not fade.
7.theology:
The body is God's craftsmanship, and delight in one's own spouse is holy (vv. 1-9; Ps 139:14; Heb 13:4). Such desire is directed to one's spouse alone, in contrast to lust (Matt 5:28).

Mature love rests in being desired (v. 10), as faith rests in Christ's love for us rather than in the strength of our love for him (1 John 4:19; Isa 62:5). Either spouse may take the lead in love, and each gives to the other (vv. 11-13; 1 Cor 7:3-4).
7.examples: A king with an army and a throne is held captive by his wife's hair, and is glad of it. A couple long married still finish each other's sentences. And a wife who books a weekend away is doing what the bride does in verse 11: making an occasion for love instead of waiting for one.

keyVerse.quote: I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.
keyVerse.note: The refrain of belonging reaches its deepest form here. The bride no longer asserts her claim on him but rests in his desire for her, and the word for desire, last heard in the curse of Genesis 3:16, now speaks of love restored. It is the believer’s deepest rest too: not the strength of our hold on Christ, but his love for us.

7.reflection:
In verses 1–9 the husband names his wife’s beauty specifically and gratefully, as “the work of a master hand” (v. 1). How does seeing the body as God’s craftsmanship free us both from lust and from shame about our own bodies?

Compare the three forms of the refrain (2:16; 6:3; 7:10). What has changed in the bride? Why is “his desire is for me” such a deep place of rest, in marriage and with Christ (1 John 4:19)?

In verses 11–12 the bride takes the initiative and makes an occasion for love. What occasions could you make for love in your marriage, your friendships or your walk with God?

Verse 13 speaks of fruits “new as well as old” laid up for the beloved. What old treasures and new joys could you bring out this week for someone you love, or for the Lord?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Oh That You Were Like a Brother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love longs to be open, rests in an embrace that has outlasted every trial, and still guards its proper time. The bride wishes she could kiss her beloved in the street as freely as a sister kisses a brother, and bring him home to her mother’s house to share her best (vv. 1–2). His embrace is just as it was in 2:6, after everything that has happened since (v. 3). And for the third time she charges the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases (v. 4). The book most frank about desire is also the book that most often warns against waking it too soon, because only what is precious needs guarding.
verseByVerse.theology: Love longs to be public as well as private, and still guards its proper time.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you were like a brother to me who nursed at my mother's breasts! If I found you outside, I would kiss you, and none would despise me. I would lead you and bring you into the house of my mother— she who used to teach me. I would give you spiced wine to drink, the juice of my pomegranate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She longs to show her love as freely in public as in private, and to give him the best she has.

Oh that you were like a brother to me! In her world a woman could kiss a brother in the street and no one would think anything of it; to kiss a husband in public would be scandalous. So she wishes, oddly and touchingly, that he were like her brother, not instead of her husband, but so that her love could be shown anywhere.

Love wants to be open. Something is wrong when a marriage is affectionate behind closed doors and cold in company, or warm in company and cold at home.

Into the house of my mother. She would bring him home, to the house where she was taught, and give him her best: spiced wine, the juice of her pomegranate. Love gives what it has.

Uncertain wording. “She who used to teach me” can also be read you would teach me; the Hebrew verb form allows either. Either way, home is the place of learning love.

verseByVerse.quote: His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me! I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem, that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After everything, his embrace is the same, and love so strong must still wait for its time.

His left hand is under my head. The words of 2:6 return. Whatever has happened in between, the closed door, the night search, the beating, the embrace is the same: after everything, here they still are.

The refrain once more. And the refrain for the third time (2:7; 3:5), the most repeated sentence in the book. A book this frank about desire says three times: do not awaken it before its time. The two are not in tension. Only what is precious needs guarding, and the Song is about to tell us how strong this love is. To the young and to all who wait, the refrain is not a scowl but a kindness; and where love was woken too soon, the Bridegroom’s mercy is greater than the past (see the note on v. 10).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here is the summit of the Song: love sealed by covenant is as strong as death, kindled by God himself, unquenchable and beyond price. The bride comes up from the wilderness leaning on her beloved and recalls where love was awakened (v. 5). Then she asks to be set as a seal on his heart and arm, for love is strong as death, its jealousy fierce as the grave, its flame “the very flame of the LORD”, probably the only time God is named in the book (v. 6). Many waters cannot quench it, and anyone who tried to buy it with all his wealth would be scorned (v. 7). It is the Song’s clearest window onto the love of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The Song's climax: love that death cannot break, floods cannot drown and money cannot buy, because its flame is from the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is that coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved? Under the apple tree I awakened you. There your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She comes up out of the wilderness leaning on her beloved, and remembers where their love began.

Leaning on her beloved. A question from onlookers, echoing 3:6, where a royal procession came up from the wilderness in clouds of perfume. This time it is a woman walking, leaning on her beloved. The grand procession has given way to two people coming home, and the picture is tender at the human level first: the strength a husband and wife become to each other over years.

The pilgrim’s journey. The image has comforted Christians for centuries, and rightly, because the pilgrim’s journey through the wilderness of this world is made leaning on Christ. Israel too came through the wilderness carried by the LORD “as a man carries his son” (Deuteronomy 1:31).

Under the apple tree. Where love was awakened is the very place where his mother gave birth to him. Life and love belong to the same ground: marriage is where new life comes from, and every beloved was once someone’s newborn child. And “awakened” echoes the refrain: here love has been awakened in its proper season.

Uncertain wording. Who speaks the second half of the verse is not stated. The Hebrew pronouns show a woman speaking to a man, so it is most likely the bride, recalling where their love began.

verseByVerse.quote: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She asks to be bound to his heart and life for ever, because love is as strong and unyielding as death, a fire kindled by the LORD himself.

Set me as a seal upon your heart. Here is the summit of the Song. A seal was a signet, a ring or cylinder carrying its owner’s name. She asks to be what he carries closest: on the heart, where love is felt, and on the arm, where it is seen and where it works. Israel was told to bind God’s words on the hand (Deuteronomy 6:8), and the high priest carried the names of the tribes on his heart when he went in before God (Exodus 28:29).

Love is strong as death. Why does she ask it? Because love is that serious. Nothing is as irresistible as death; no one refuses it. Love is like that: it lays hold of a person and will not let go. And “jealousy is fierce as the grave”: not petty suspicion, but the rightful passion of love that will not share the beloved. Love by its nature is exclusive.

What it means that love is jealous. We hear the word jealous and picture someone insecure and possessive, so it unsettles us that God calls himself jealous: “the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God” (Exodus 34:14). But a husband who shrugs when his wife is unfaithful does not love her more; his love has already died. The more you love someone, the more you burn against whatever is destroying them. God’s jealousy is that kind: not insecurity, but passion for the good of the one he loves. Paul felt the same fire for the church: “I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). So when something else begins to take Christ’s place in your heart, a career, a screen, a person, read the unrest that follows not as a God merely displeased, but as a Bridegroom who will not let you go.

The very flame of the LORD. Here, probably for the only time in the book, God is named. If so, that phrase tells us where this fire comes from: human love is not merely chemistry or a social arrangement, but a flame kindled from the love of God himself. “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

Strong as death, and stronger. Here the Song reaches farthest toward Christ. Marriage was made to picture Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:25–32), and Christ’s love was strong as death, and stronger. God’s jealous love burned hottest at the cross: Christ would not leave his bride to sin and death, so he went into death to take her back, and came out again. He carries his people as a seal: “Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands” (Isaiah 49:16). And he has sealed them to himself: believers were “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (Ephesians 1:13).

Isn’t the Bible’s view of sex too narrow? Many assume that Christianity is embarrassed by sex, forbidding much and celebrating nothing, and the church has sometimes earned that reputation. But the modern alternative has its own troubles. On one side sex has been made trivial, an appetite like hunger, to be satisfied with whoever is willing: the woman of Proverbs who eats, wipes her mouth and says she has done no wrong (Proverbs 30:20). On the other it has been made ultimate: the right lover will complete me, heal my past and give my life its meaning. Trivial and divine at once, it can bear neither weight. Even some who do not share the Christian faith now say so; the writer Louise Perry, arguing as a secular feminist, has contended that the sexual revolution served men’s appetites far better than women’s interests. The Song refuses both mistakes. Desire here is too glorious to be trivial, a flame of the LORD, and too strong to be a god, which is why it must be sealed by covenant. And it points beyond itself: only someone who already has the love of the Bridegroom who proved stronger than death can enjoy human love without demanding that it save him.

Uncertain wording. “The very flame of the LORD” is one Hebrew word ending in -yah, a short form of the LORD’s name. It may only mean a mighty flame (so the KJV, a most vehement flame), since Hebrew can use God’s name to say “very great”; but many think the name is meant, and the ESV takes it so. In the same verse jealousy may be rendered “ardor”, and the grave is in Hebrew “as Sheol” (ESV notes), the realm of the dead, which never says “Enough” (Proverbs 30:15–16).
verseByVerse.note: On the seal as a sign of belonging, compare Haggai 2:23, where the LORD makes Zerubbabel like a signet ring.

verseByVerse.quote: Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods drown it. If a man offered for love all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No flood can put out this love and no fortune can buy it: it can only be given and received.

Many waters cannot quench love. Fire is put out by water; this fire is not. Pour the sea on it and it burns. That is a promise to hold in the hard years. Floods do come to a marriage: illness, poverty, grief, betrayal, the slow wearing of time. Real love is not extinguished by them, and many marriages that fail had let the fire burn low long before the floods came. But where a marriage was broken by a spouse’s betrayal, desertion or abuse, the fault is not the faithful one’s, and Christ’s love for the wounded does not fail with it.

Firm ground. For the believer this is the firm ground under everything. Nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). Having loved his own, “he loved them to the end” (John 13:1). In Israel’s poems many waters stand for overwhelming trouble and death (Psalm 18:16); Christ went down into those waters for his people, and his love came up unquenched.

Love cannot be bought. A man who tried to purchase it with everything he owned would only show that he did not know what love is. That is why the gospel is not a purchase. No one buys God’s love; it is given. And the only right response is the merchant’s who found one pearl of great value and “sold all that he had and bought it” (Matthew 13:46): not paying for love, but letting go of everything else for its sake.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Vineyard and the Final Call
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Song ends with love kept, love owned and love still longing. Her brothers wonder how to protect their little sister until the day she is spoken for (vv. 8–9). The bride answers from her own life: she was a wall, kept for one man, and in his eyes she found peace (v. 10). Solomon may keep his vineyard let out for a thousand pieces of silver; her one vineyard, her own love, is worth more (vv. 11–12). Then the lovers speak for the last time: he longs to hear her voice, and she calls him to come quickly (vv. 13–14). The Song ends not with a conclusion but with a call, as Scripture itself does.
verseByVerse.theology: Purity kept, love owned and not sold, and a last call for the beloved to come.

verseByVerse.quote: We have a little sister, and she has no breasts. What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is spoken for? If she is a wall, we will build on her a battlement of silver, but if she is a door, we will enclose her with boards of cedar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her brothers want to protect their little sister until her wedding day, honouring her if she keeps herself and guarding her if she does not.

We have a little sister. Other voices now: her brothers, probably the same brothers who made her work the vineyards in 1:6, asking what to do for a younger sister on the day she is spoken for. If she proves a wall, keeping herself, they will crown it with silver. If a door, open to anyone, they will board her up. Their instinct is protection.

Preparing the young. Parents and churches still face this question: what shall we do for the young, before they are promised in marriage? The Song’s answer is neither neglect nor imprisonment, but preparation and honour. The aim is not merely to prevent something but to keep something for its time, so that it can be given whole. “For this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3), and the God who wills our holiness is the one who makes us holy by his Spirit.

Uncertain wording. Most take the door as the opposite of the wall, open to anyone. Some read both lines as honour: a wall crowned with silver, a door panelled in fine cedar, the brothers adorning their sister whichever she proves to be. The call to guard and honour the young stands either way.

verseByVerse.quote: I was a wall, and my breasts were like towers; then I was in his eyes as one who finds peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She kept herself for one man, and in his eyes she found peace: purity is not the enemy of passion but its protection.

I was a wall. She answers for herself: she kept herself, and was not a door open to everyone. Now she is in his eyes “as one who finds peace”. The Hebrew for peace, shalom, sounds like the names Solomon and Shulammite.

Purity and passion. She does not say, “I was a wall, so I missed out.” The woman who kept the gate locked is the woman of chapters 4 to 7, who knows love at its richest. Purity is not the enemy of passion. It is its protection.

For those who were not a wall. The gospel has a word for those who cannot say this. Christ makes the unclean clean, and presents his bride without blemish (Ephesians 5:27). No past puts a person beyond that mercy. And anyone whose wall was broken down by another, through abuse, carries no guilt for it: the shame belongs to the one who did it.

Uncertain wording. Finds may be rendered “brings out” (ESV note): she found peace, or she brought peace to him. Both are true of a faithful wife.

verseByVerse.quote: Solomon had a vineyard at Baal-hamon; he let out the vineyard to keepers; each one was to bring for its fruit a thousand pieces of silver. My vineyard, my very own, is before me; you, O Solomon, may have the thousand, and the keepers of the fruit two hundred.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solomon may keep his profitable vineyard; her one love is worth more to her than all a king’s wealth.

Solomon had a vineyard. A vineyard let out to tenants for a thousand pieces of silver: love treated like an estate managed for profit. Solomon had vineyards of that kind. Scripture records his seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines plainly and says they turned his heart away (1 Kings 11:3–4). It reports polygamy without approving it, and the Song’s own picture is one man and one woman, each the other’s only one (6:3, 9).

My vineyard, my very own. And the bride speaks with quiet magnificence: keep your thousand, Solomon. She has one vineyard, her own love and her own husband, and she would not trade it for a royal estate.

How she began. Remember how she began: “they made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I have not kept!” (1:6). The book that opened with a woman who had no vineyard of her own ends with her holding it, worth more to her than everything Solomon owns. One faithful marriage is worth more than a palace full of wives.

Uncertain wording. The name Baal-hamon means something like lord of a multitude or owner of wealth, perhaps chosen for its meaning. Most hear the bride in verse 12, though some hear the bridegroom; either way, one loved vineyard outweighs a thousand pieces of silver.
verseByVerse.note: Baal-hamon is otherwise unknown. A thousand pieces of silver was a great sum.

verseByVerse.quote: O you who dwell in the gardens, with companions listening for your voice; let me hear it. Make haste, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of spices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He longs to hear her voice; she calls him to come quickly: the Song ends not in a conclusion but in longing, as the Bible itself does.

Let me hear it. The bridegroom’s last words ask to hear her voice, as in 2:14. Of everything he could ask for, he asks for her speech. Love never tires of the beloved’s voice.

Make haste, my beloved. And the bride has the last word, as she had the first (1:2). It is not a conclusion but a call: come quickly, like a young stag over the fragrant hills. The Song ends in longing, the lovers still reaching for each other. That is honest. This side of eternity love is never finished; it always wants more.

How the Bible ends. And the Bible ends the same way. The Spirit and the Bride say to the Bridegroom, “Come” (Revelation 22:17), and he answers, “Surely I am coming soon”, and the church replies, “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). The last prayer of the Song and the last prayer of Scripture are the same prayer. Whoever has learned to say “Make haste, my beloved” to a husband or a wife has learned something of what it means to wait for Christ; and whoever has learned to say it to Christ has found the love that is strong as death, and stronger.

8.title: Love Is Strong as Death
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 is the Song’s last movement. Love has been longed for, won, lost and restored, and the bride has just rested in “his desire is for me” (7:10). Now the book gathers up its themes, reaches its summit and ends.

The message. Married love is a fire kindled by God: strong as death, unquenchable by floods, beyond the reach of money; so it must be sealed by covenant and guarded until its time. The bride who kept herself prizes her one vineyard above a king’s wealth, and the Song closes not with a happy ending but with a cry of longing: “Make haste, my beloved” (v. 14).

Why it was said. Israel lived among peoples who made sex a commodity or a religion, and its own king gathered a thousand women and lost his heart (see the introduction). The Song answers with one faithful love, guarded, sealed and freely given, and gently puts Solomon’s thousand in its place (vv. 11–12).

How the chapter makes its case. She longs to show her love openly; his embrace is as it was; and the charge not to awaken love before its time sounds for the last time [vv. 1–4]. Then the summit: she comes up from the wilderness leaning on her beloved, asks to be set as a seal on his heart, and declares that love is strong as death, the very flame of the LORD, which floods cannot quench nor wealth buy [vv. 5–7]. Last come her brothers’ care for their little sister, her own testimony that she was a wall and found peace, her one vineyard set against Solomon’s thousand, and a final exchange: he longs to hear her voice, and she calls him to come [vv. 8–14].

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, by the need it exposes, and by promise. The love the Song calls strong as death proved stronger than death when Christ went into death for his bride and came back. He carries his people on his heart and has sealed them with his Spirit (Ephesians 1:13); his love cannot be bought, only received, and nothing “will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39). And the Song’s last prayer is the Bible’s last prayer: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).

For us. Guard love until its time, and where it was not guarded, come to the Bridegroom who makes clean. Tend the fire in your marriage through every flood, and never try to buy or force what can only be given. And learn to long for Christ’s coming as the bride longs for her beloved.
8.theology:
Love is to be guarded until its time (v. 4), and it must be guarded because it is strong as death and exclusive by nature (v. 6). Its flame is kindled by God himself, probably the one mention of the LORD in the book (v. 6; 1 John 4:19).

Love cannot be drowned or bought (v. 7): Christ's love for his people cannot be separated from them (Rom 8:39; John 13:1), and it is given, never purchased (Matt 13:46). Purity kept is honoured and brings peace (vv. 9-10; 1 Thess 4:3), and where it was not kept, Christ still presents his bride without blemish (Eph 5:27).

The Song ends in longing for the beloved to come, as Scripture ends with the Bride calling the Bridegroom (vv. 13-14; Rev 22:17, 20).
8.examples: An elderly couple walking slowly home from church, one leaning on the other, is the picture of verse 5. A wedding ring worn for fifty years is a seal set on the arm. And a man who tried to buy love with everything he owned would only prove he had never known it.

keyVerse.quote: Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy is fierce as the grave. Its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: This is the summit of the Song, and probably the one place in it where God is named. Love sealed by covenant is as strong and unyielding as death, because its fire is kindled by the LORD himself. Christ’s love proved stronger still: he went into death for his bride, and he carries his people as a seal upon his heart.

8.reflection:
The charge not to “stir up or awaken love until it pleases” comes a third time (v. 4). Why does a book so frank about desire also warn so often about its timing? How can a church help its young people keep love for its time, and show mercy where it was not kept?

Verse 6 calls love “strong as death” and jealous. How does the jealousy of God differ from human possessiveness (Exodus 34:14; 2 Corinthians 11:2)? What might Christ’s jealous love be calling you away from?

Love can be neither quenched nor bought (v. 7). How does this help us face the floods that come to a marriage, and how does it free us from trying to earn God’s love (Romans 8:38–39)?

The Song and the Bible both end with a call for the beloved to come (v. 14; Revelation 22:20). How much do you long for Christ’s return, and what would grow that longing?
